articles.title: I built a LEGO builder for my son with Claude. The hard part was making sure no brick floats
articles.description: I built Mister Blocks for my son. We have the classic giant box of mixed LEGO: sets long broken up, instructions long gone. Every time he asked "what can I build?", I didn't have a good answer. Now he takes a photo of the pile, and a few minutes later there are a few builds made only from the bricks in that photo, with 3D step-by-step instructions he can turn, zoom and print. The first working version came out of the very first prompt to Claude. The next few days went into the part nobody warns you about: making sure the build actually holds together in real plastic. This post is about that part. The pipeline There is no framework. It's a handful of Vercel serverless functions in plain Node, MongoDB for sessions, Cloudflare R2 for images and PDFs, and three.js for the 3D view: api/sessions/[id]/recognize photo -> inventory (every piece: kind, size in studs, color) api/sessions/[id]/design inventory -> one model (parts with x/y/z positions + steps) api/sessions/[id]/chat "make it a tow truck" -> a changed model, same checks Recognize. Claude (Opus 5.5) looks at the photo and returns structured JSON. Each piece gets an id (B3 is a brick, P7 a plate, W1 a wheel), its size in studs, its height in plates and its color. If it miscounts, you can correct it in the chat ("there are 48 of the 2×4s") and the inventory is reconciled without breaking the ids the models already use. Design. Claude gets the inventory and returns a model: every part placed on a grid (x and z in studs, y in plates, where a brick is 3 plates tall), plus which step it goes in. And that's where it gets interesting, because a language model's first answer is almost right very often. Almost right in LEGO means a brick floating in mid-air. The stud checker Every model goes through a checker before anyone sees it. It's one plain JS file (core.js), and the server and the browser load the exact same file, so what the page shows and what the server accepts can't disagree. It checks the things that make a build fail in your hands: Every piece is held by studs. A piece's bottom cells have to land on studs of something below it, or the piece has to sit on the table. Slopes only have studs on their top row, so the checker knows that too. No two pieces occupy the same space. Only pieces you actually have. Every part has to exist in the inventory, be of the same kind, and be used only once. Wheels can turn. Nothing may come lower than the deck inside a tire's zone, except the mudguard over its own tire. The checker returns problems in plain English, and they go straight back to Claude: Up to three rounds. In practice most models pass in one or two. This loop does more for quality than any amount of prompt tuning did: the model is good at fixing a specific, named problem, and much worse at avoiding every possible problem up front. Steps you can actually build The next surprise was in the instructions, not the model. A model can be perfectly valid at the end and still impossible to build in the given order, for example when step 3 places a piece that is only held by a plate that arrives in step 5. You'd be holding that piece in the air. So there's a second pass (fixOrder) that walks the steps. For every group of new pieces in a step, it checks that they clip onto something already built or stand on the table. If they don't, it pulls the holding piece forward into that step, the way a real builder would put the plate on over the pieces it holds. Moving a piece earlier never breaks an earlier step, and a later step can only gain support, so the pass is safe to repeat until nothing changes. Rules learned from a kid's truck The prompt has a section of rules that came from real builds, mostly from my son's own truck. For example, the chassis that works: two wheel plates in a row, joined by a 2-wide strip of plates, a mudguard over each wheel set one stud outward, and the deck resting on the mudguards plus a center block. Before that rule existed, a lot of generated cars had decks that sat on the tires. The rules are written as plain sentences, the same way you'd explain them to a person. The viewer The 3D viewer is a small three.js file shared by the build page, the guides and the print view. Every brick gets a gentle sheen and highlighted edges, so it reads as plastic rather than as flat boxes. You drag to turn, scroll to zoom, and step through the build one step at a time; pointing at a step in the list lights up its pieces and fades everything else back. Every guide can be printed as a booklet or saved as a PDF, and the guides you've opened work offline. Prompt mode and bigger builds Not everyone has a pile handy, so you can also describe a build in words. A few of my favourites, each a free guide you can turn in 3D, step through and print: Boston Dynamics Spot, with its arm The yellow-and-black robot dog on four backward-bending legs, reaching for a valve on a factory floor. 150 pieces, 13 steps. Build it → SpongeBob's Pineapple House The pineapple under the sea: round, wider in the middle, with the blue door and a crown of leaves. 237 pieces, 18 steps. Build it → Porsche Mission S Porsche's vision car in white, with the black canopy and the full-width red light bar. The big one: 965 pieces in 73 steps. Build it → (Want something quicker? There's also a 69-piece version.) Mega Dragonite A voxel sculpture of the dragon Pokémon: 1,315 pieces in 121 steps. Build it → More in the gallery. The large sculptures go through a different path. A 3D shape is described as ellipsoids, limbs and tubes, packed into standard bricks on a plate base, and given clear supports until it holds. Then it goes through the same stud check. Cost Each build takes a few minutes and costs a couple of dollars in API calls. Every Claude call's tokens and cost are logged to MongoDB, and there's a per-visitor daily limit plus a site-wide daily budget, so a busy day can't turn into a surprise bill. Try it It's free: misterblocks.com. Snap your pile and see what it comes up with. I'd love to hear what you build, and especially what it got wrong. Unofficial fan project. articles.title: Your SOC 2 report doesn't answer a single AI question
articles.description: A SOC 2 Type II is a beautiful document. It proves you control access, you monitor systems, you manage change. Auditors love it, procurement accepts it, everyone relaxes. Then a customer asks three questions: Which model versions processed our data in the last 90 days? Can you show the specific decision your AI made about our user, and replay the inputs that produced it? Who could edit those records, and how would we detect it if they did? SOC 2 has no criteria for any of them. Its trust services criteria were written for systems where logic is deterministic and humans write the code. Your inference stack breaks all three assumptions: the logic is statistical, the "code" changes when you swap a checkpoint, and your agents call tools you didn't hardcode. This is why ISO 42001 exists, and why the AICPA has been drafting AI-specific guidance. But you don't need to wait for a framework to fix the gap. The engineering is concrete: Pin model + version + prompt template ID on every inference record Store records append-only, with a hash chain so edits are detectable Capture the policy version in force at decision time Keep retention long enough to answer "last quarter" without shrugging None of that is hard. What's hard is realizing your SOC 2 gave you false confidence, and the first customer who asks will find out before you do. Which of the three questions above could you answer today, with artifacts?

articles.title: Resolving Architectural Tension in State Management by Moving from Client SPAs to Server-Driven Approaches
articles.description: For over a decade, web architecture has swung violently toward the browser. We loaded the client with massive JavaScript bundles, forcing the browser to shoulder the burden of routing, state synchronization, and business logic. But this pendulum swing was not an accident of history; it was driven by specific technological catalysts and a growing friction that is now fracturing developer workflows. The Catalysts of Client-Side Bloat The migration of state and logic into the browser was accelerated by two major forces: The Rise of Component-Driven Frameworks: The mainstream adoption of React, Angular, and Vue decoupled UI rendering from the document lifecycle, turning browsers into full-fledged virtual machines executing complex reconciliation algorithms. The Decoupling of APIs: The industry-wide pivot toward headless architectures meant servers were reduced to dumb JSON endpoints, pushing data shaping, validation, and state caching directly onto client devices. However, this shift created a severe mechanical failure mode: distributed state synchronization. When client and server maintain separate state trees, network latency and intermittent connectivity cause state drift. The browser must continuously serialize payloads, execute redundant validation routines (duplicating server-side rules in JavaScript), and manage asynchronous cache invalidation. This friction heats up network pipelines, inflates memory footprints on resource-constrained mobile devices, and fractures team velocity under the weight of complex build toolchains. Evaluating Architectural Trade-Offs To resolve this tension, we must critically evaluate the two primary paradigms: Architectural Model Core Mechanism Failure Mode / Breaking Condition Heavy Client SPA State lives in the browser; client fetches raw data via REST/GraphQL and executes local rendering logic. Breaks down under heavy network latency, low-end mobile hardware constraints, and excessive bundle size growth leading to long Time-to-Interactive (TTI). Server-Driven Approach (e.g., LiveView) State lives on the server; UI diffs are pushed over persistent WebSocket connections, retaining client-side power only for specialized DOM manipulation (e.g., canvas rendering). Breaks down at massive horizontal scale without sticky sessions, or in offline-first environments where persistent socket connectivity cannot be guaranteed. Decision Framework for Architecture Selection Choosing where application logic belongs requires a strict operational rule: If your application requires rich, offline-first client interactions, local canvas manipulation, or complex client-side graphics (such as CAD tools, audio editors, or heavy data grids like AG Grid), then retain a client-heavy or hybrid architecture. However, if your application is primarily CRUD-driven, workflow-oriented, or constrained by team size and synchronization overhead, then a server-driven paradigm (like Phoenix LiveView) is optimal because it eliminates state duplication and collapses the network boundary. The typical choice error engineers make is treating architecture as a religious binary rather than a mechanical trade-off. Over-indexing on client SPAs for standard enterprise dashboards introduces accidental complexity—duplicating business logic across languages and inflating maintenance costs—long before scale actually demands it. The Hidden Costs of Client-Side Complexity When software architecture defaults to heavy client-side Single Page Applications (SPAs) for standard CRUD workflows, it introduces a cascade of hidden mechanical costs. By moving state engines and validation logic directly into the browser, engineering teams inadvertently subject runtime environments to severe performance and synchronization friction. The Mechanics of Distributed State Drift and Serialization Overhead In a heavy client architecture, the browser functions as a disconnected virtual machine, executing complex reconciliation algorithms while holding its own isolated copy of application state. This creates a dual-state topology: one state tree lives in server memory, and another mirrors it inside the client heap. The mechanical consequence of this separation is constant state serialization and deserialization across the network boundary. Every interaction requires structured data to be packed into JSON strings, pushed across HTTP or WebSocket layers, unpacked, processed, and re-synchronized. Under intermittent network latency or on low-end mobile hardware, this cyclic parse-and-allocate pressure starves the main JavaScript thread, directly spiking Time-to-Interactive (TTI) metrics and causing frame drops. When network packets drop or lag, state divergence fractures consistency, forcing complex optimistic updates and rollback heuristics that bloat the client-side codebase with fragile reconciliation code. Validation Duplication and Logic Decay Shifting state management to the frontend forces structural code duplication: business rules and validation schemas must be written twice—once in TypeScript or JavaScript for the browser, and mirrored in Go, Python, or Ruby on the server. This duplication creates a structural failure mode: validation drift. When a business rule changes, developers frequently update the client-side validation while lagging on the server-side counterpart (or vice versa). Because HTTP requests can be intercepted and modified via browser developer tools, relying on client-side logic for security or structural integrity permits malformed payloads to bypass front-end checks entirely. The system breaks under bad inputs because the server-side validation layer acts as a loose secondary net rather than an authoritative gatekeeper. Architectural Decision Framework: When Client SPAs Break Down To evaluate where state truly belongs, architectures must be judged by their failure modes rather than their default trendiness. Standard enterprise dashboards and CRUD workflows do not require local state engines; forcing them into client SPAs generates accidental complexity. Retain Client-Heavy / Hybrid Architecture When: Applications demand offline-first resilience, heavy local canvas manipulation, or sub-millisecond local rendering for complex data grids and code editors (such as Monaco, AG Grid, or CAD tools). Here, the local CPU is utilized to bypass network round-trip latency. Adopt Server-Driven Architecture When: Applications are primarily workflow-driven or CRUD-oriented. Utilizing models like Phoenix LiveView keeps application state resident on the server, pushing minimal DOM diffs over persistent WebSockets. This collapses the network boundary and eradicates state synchronization friction. Typical Choice Errors and Boundary Conditions The most pervasive architectural choice error is defaulting to client SPAs for enterprise CRUD dashboards out of habit or resume-driven development. This introduces massive build toolchain bloat, inflated bundle sizes, and redundant synchronization code before business scale or user interaction complexity demands it. However, server-driven approaches are not a universal panacea. They break down under specific physical and operational conditions: Massive Horizontal Scaling Without Sticky Sessions: Because server-driven frameworks like LiveView maintain active socket state in server memory, scaling requires robust session affinity; otherwise, load balancer redistribution severs active connections and flushes user state. Offline-First Environments: If an application must operate reliably during intermittent or total network disconnection, server-driven sockets fail outright, necessitating client-side local storage engines. Decision Rule: If an application's core value proposition relies on offline autonomy or heavy local pixel manipulation, utilize a client-heavy architecture. If the application is network-tethered, CRUD-centric, and bottlenecked by team maintenance overhead, adopt a server-driven architecture to eliminate state duplication at the source. The Counter-Revolution: Server-Driven UI and Hybrid Models For over a decade, the software industry treated the browser as a remote virtual machine, offloading rendering logic and application state onto client hardware. This monopoly is now fracturing under its own weight. Emerging paradigms like Phoenix LiveView, HTMX, and React Server Components represent a direct counter-revolution, shoving execution and state back across the network boundary to the server where they historically resided. Mechanics of the Server-Driven Shift In a heavy client SPA, every user interaction triggers local event handlers that mutate local state, execute reconciliation algorithms, serialize data into JSON payloads, and fire HTTP requests over the wire. This creates a dual-state topology where the client heap and server memory mirror each other imperfectly, leading to serialization overhead and heavy parse-and-allocate pressure on the main JavaScript thread under intermittent network latency or on low-end hardware. Server-driven architectures like Phoenix LiveView short-circuit this mechanical drag. By maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection, state resides exclusively in server memory. When an interaction occurs, only minor DOM diffs are calculated on the server and pushed down the wire as compact binary or text frames. The browser client is reduced to a thin rendering conduit, dropping CPU cycles spent on local state synchronization, client-side routing logic, and redundant validation schemas. The Hybrid Compromise: Preserving Specialized Client Capabilities A common engineering fear is that adopting server-driven patterns forces a regression into crude, multi-page HTML forms that destroy rich user experiences. This is a false dichotomy. As developers note in modern architectural discussions, keeping state on the server does not mean discarding JavaScript entirely. Specialized client-side components—such as code editors (Monaco), massive data grids (AG Grid), or high-frequency charting engines (Chart.js)—require sub-millisecond local rendering loops and heavy canvas or WebGL manipulation that cannot tolerate network round-trip latency. The correct architectural boundary isolates these specialized execution engines on the client while centralizing core business logic, routing, and workflow state on the server. Decision Dominance: When to Deploy Server-Driven vs. Client-Heavy Architectures Architectural choices must be governed by mechanical constraints rather than industry fads. Defaulting to a heavy client SPA for standard enterprise dashboards introduces accidental complexity, language-duplicated validation logic, and inflated bundle sizes before scale or interaction complexity demands it. Decision Rule: Use Server-Driven Architecture (e.g., LiveView, HTMX) when: Applications are primarily CRUD-driven, workflow-oriented, or bottlenecked by team coordination and state synchronization overhead. If your app spends most of its life syncing local state with a database via REST endpoints, server-driven architectures eliminate state duplication at the source and collapse the network boundary. Retain Client-Heavy / Hybrid Architectures when: The application demands offline-first resilience, sub-millisecond local rendering loops, heavy canvas/WebGL manipulation, or localized data manipulation that cannot survive network partitioning. Breaking Conditions and Failure Modes Every architecture has a breaking point. Server-driven frameworks like LiveView fail catastrophically under two specific conditions: massive horizontal scaling without sticky sessions and total offline environments. When a load balancer redistributes WebSocket traffic across multiple application servers without persistent sticky routing, active connections are severed, flushing user state resident in server memory and throwing fatal connection errors. Similarly, in unstable or offline network topologies, severing the persistent socket connection immediately freezes the interface, whereas a client-side SPA can continue operating against local cache until connectivity is restored. Striking the Right Balance: A Modern Architectural Decision Framework Architectural paralysis in modern web engineering stems from a false binary: treating applications as either universally server-rendered or entirely client-bound. Choosing the wrong paradigm introduces severe mechanical friction. Defaulting to a heavy client single-page application (SPA) for standard CRUD or workflow software triggers a dual-state topology, forcing the client heap and server memory to constantly synchronize over JSON payloads. This architectural tax exacts a heavy price: cyclic parse-and-allocate pressure starves the main JavaScript thread, inflating Time-to-Interactive (TTI) metrics and creating validation drift as business rules decay independently across backend services and frontend runtimes. To eliminate this accidental complexity, engineers must evaluate architectural fit through hard system constraints rather than framework fashion. The decision space relies on a strict boundary rule: Deploy Server-Driven Architectures (e.g., Phoenix LiveView) When: Applications are primarily network-tethered, CRUD-driven, or workflow-oriented. By keeping application state resident exclusively in server memory and pushing compact binary or text diffs over persistent WebSockets, this approach collapses the network boundary, strips out client-side routing overhead, and completely eradicates state synchronization bugs at the source. Retain Client-Heavy / Hybrid Architectures When: Core requirements demand offline autonomy, sub-millisecond local rendering, or heavy canvas/WebGL manipulation (such as code editors, CAD tools, or high-frequency data grids). Here, keeping computation local bypasses the physical latency of network round-trips, ensuring zero-frame-drop performance during intensive local pixel manipulation. The table below contrasts the mechanical trade-offs of these competing paradigms: Metric Client-Heavy SPA Server-Driven (LiveView) State Location Split across client heap and server database Centralized entirely in server RAM Network Payload Raw JSON over REST/GraphQL; high serialization cost Compact DOM diffs over persistent WebSockets Primary Failure Mode State divergence, bundle bloat, validation drift Connection drop on unsticky load balancers Every architectural choice carries a specific breaking condition. Server-driven models fail catastrophically under missing sticky session routing in horizontal scaling topologies; when a load balancer redistributes traffic to a new node, the active WebSocket connection is severed, instantly flushing the user's in-memory state and throwing fatal connection errors. They also break in total offline environments where network partitioning freezes the user interface. Conversely, client SPAs fail mechanically under intermittent network latency and low-end hardware constraints where large bundle sizes starve the main thread. The definitive professional judgment is clear: stop defaulting enterprise dashboards and workflow applications to client-side SPAs. Match the execution engine to the domain reality—centralize core logic on the server to eliminate duplication, and reserve the browser strictly for specialized local performance loops.

articles.title: What Is SIP? Sessions, the Handshake and Call Failures
articles.description: SIP shows up the moment you wire a phone number to anything: a PBX, a contact centre, a voice AI agent. And the first time a call fails, you're staring at a trace full of INVITEs, 1xx and 4xx codes. This post gives you the mental model to read that trace: what a session, dialog and transaction are, what the handshake protects, and how to tell which stage broke. SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is the IETF signalling standard that sets up, changes, and ends real-time calls over IP. It finds the other party, agrees on codecs and addresses using SDP, then steps aside while RTP carries the audio. SIP itself never carries a caller's voice. This guide separates three terms that most explainers blur: session, dialog, and transaction. It then shows what the handshake protects, what SIP does when a message goes missing, and how to read a failed call by the stage where it stopped. Note: Key takeaways SIP controls calls, and RTP carries them. A call can connect perfectly and still be silent, because the two protocols can take different network paths. A session is not a dialog. The session is the media exchange, the dialog is the signalling relationship, and a transaction is one request with its responses. The handshake is INVITE, 200 OK, ACK. SIP needs the third step because a person can take many seconds to answer. 32 seconds is a useful clue. With default timers, a 200 OK that never gets its ACK ends in a BYE at that point. In India, what you signal matters. TRAI's rules on number series and automated calls apply to the calls your trunk sets up. What is SIP? RFC 3261 defines SIP as an application-layer control protocol for creating, modifying, and terminating sessions. Published in June 2002, it replaced the original RFC 2543 of March 1999. It remains the base SIP standard, with extensions added by later RFCs. SIP messages are readable text, and their request and response model resembles HTTP. A request names a method, such as INVITE, and a response returns a numeric status, such as 200 OK. The IANA SIP registry lists 14 methods as of its October 2026 update, though a basic call needs only a few. SIP reaches well beyond desk phones. GetVoIP's overview lists uses including VoLTE, SIP trunking, and video conferencing. Each use relies on the same division of labour: Protocol Job on a call Defined in SIP Finds the party, rings, accepts, changes, and ends the call RFC 3261 SDP Describes the media: codecs, address, port, and direction RFC 8866 Offer/answer Sets how two sides use SDP to reach agreement RFC 3264 RTP Carries the audio packets RFC 3550 SRTP Encrypts and authenticates those packets RFC 3711 Who takes part in SIP signalling? A user agent is anything that starts or answers calls, such as a softphone, PBX, or voice AI service. A proxy routes requests onward. A registrar accepts REGISTER requests and records where a user can be reached. A session border controller sits at a network edge, and RFC 5853 catalogues its usual jobs, including topology hiding and NAT traversal. The diagram follows the classic example from section 4 of RFC 3261. Notice that the audio never touches the proxies in this layout. What is a SIP session? In SIP, the session is the media exchange that signalling sets up. RFC 3261 puts it plainly: a session is a collection of participants and the media streams between them. The word gets used loosely, so check which of these two meanings you're reading. In the protocol, a session is one live media exchange, created when the offer and answer complete. In a sales quote, a "SIP session" can mean one concurrent call, the same unit as a channel. TelNet Worldwide's 2022 explainer uses the word this way. Protocol engineers then split the signalling into two more layers. VideoSDK's session guide draws a similar three-part split, and these definitions follow the RFC: Layer What it is How long it lasts How SIP identifies it Transaction One request and the responses to it Usually seconds, or longer while a phone rings The branch value in the top Via header Dialog The signalling relationship between two user agents From the first tagged response until BYE Call-ID, a local tag, and a remote tag Session The media those user agents exchange From completed offer/answer until BYE The origin line in SDP Why do the layers matter? The separation lets you describe a problem precisely. A dialog can exist before a session does. A tagged 180 Ringing creates an early dialog, even though nobody has answered. One INVITE can create several dialogs. A forking proxy can ring several devices, and each 2xx from a different device forms its own dialog. A session can change while the dialog stays. A hold or codec change gives the session a new description under the same Call-ID. Your logs can join them. Call-ID is the value to search for when you compare traces from two systems. Sizing uses the sales meaning, where one call in progress holds one channel. TRAI's February 2025 numbering recommendations note that a 2 Mbps PRI has 30 channels, and they put a SIP call at about 87 kbps with G.711 or 32 kbps with G.729. To turn call volume into channels, use the worked Erlang B example in What is SIP trunking?. What is the SIP handshake? The SIP handshake is the three-message exchange that establishes a call: INVITE, 200 OK, and ACK. RFC 3261 calls it the INVITE/200/ACK three-way handshake. Responses such as 100 Trying and 180 Ringing report progress, but they don't complete it. INVITE. The caller asks for a session and usually includes an SDP offer listing the media it can handle. 200 OK. The callee accepts and returns an SDP answer with its chosen codec and media address. ACK. The caller confirms that it received the acceptance, and the call is established. Why does SIP need a third message? Requests other than INVITE finish with a two-way exchange, but an INVITE usually waits on a person. The RFC gives that long, human-driven delay as the reason for the extra step. By the time someone answers, the caller may have gone or its network may have changed, so the callee needs proof that the caller is still there. The name invites a comparison with TCP's three-way handshake, but the two do different jobs. TCP synchronises a connection between two hosts. SIP's exchange runs at the application layer, over UDP as well as TCP. It records a person's decision to answer and completes an agreement about media. Two details surprise people when they read traces: The ACK for a 200 OK stands apart. It's a separate transaction and goes end to end, often straight to the address in the callee's Contact header. The ACK for a failure response stays within the INVITE transaction and is handled hop by hop. The offer can come later. If an INVITE has no SDP, the 200 OK carries the offer and the ACK carries the answer. This is often called delayed offer. Most developers never send the ACK by hand, because SIP stacks normally generate it. Dialogic's 2010 SIP manual, for example, describes it as automatic with an option for manual control. What happens when a handshake message is lost? SIP was built to survive packet loss on UDP, so each side resends on a timer. The chart plots what RFC 3261's default timers produce. The lower line produces a recognisable symptom. Both people talk normally for about half a minute, and then the call drops. The callee kept resending its 200 OK for 64 × T1 seconds, got no ACK, and ended the session with BYE. One likely cause is a Contact address that the ACK can't reach, such as a private address that a NAT device left in place. The upper line can't produce audio at all. No reply within 64 × T1 ends the attempt, and the timing itself tells you that something on the signalling route never answered. Other exchanges people call a SIP handshake People use the word for four different exchanges, and each one fails in its own way: Exchange Messages What it settles Typical failure Call handshake INVITE, 200 OK, ACK Call accepted and media agreed Drop at about 32 seconds Digest challenge Request, 401 or 407, then a retry with credentials Who is calling Same challenge repeats Registration REGISTER, often challenged, then 200 OK Where a user can be reached Binding expires, calls stop arriving TLS handshake TLS negotiation before any SIP message Encryption and server identity on that hop Certificate or version mismatch, with no SIP in the trace How does a SIP session change and end? The session stays open to change after the handshake. These methods cover the rest of a call's life: Method When you see it What it does REGISTER Before any call Records a user's current address PRACK During setup Makes a provisional response reliable, which matters for PSTN interworking CANCEL Before answer Abandons a ringing attempt, which draws a 487 UPDATE During setup or the call Changes session details, even before the answer re-INVITE During the call Offers a full new session description in the same dialog REFER Asks the other side to contact a third party, the basis of transfer BYE To end the call Ends the session, usually the dialog as well Hold is a useful worked example. One side sends a new offer that marks the stream sendonly. The answer agrees, and the other side stops sending audio. The Call-ID doesn't change, because only the session changed. If both sides send a re-INVITE at once, each side answers the other with 491 Request Pending. Each one then retries after a random wait. This collision is sometimes called glare. What is a SIP session timer? Base SIP has no keepalive for sessions. If a BYE is lost, a server tracking the call can't tell that it ended. RFC 4028 solves this with periodic re-INVITE or UPDATE requests, negotiated through the Session-Expires and Min-SE headers. It recommends 30 minutes for Session-Expires, sets a floor of 90 seconds, and recommends refreshing at the halfway point. A value that is too low draws a 422 response. When calls drop at a regular interval, check whether a refresh was sent and answered. How do you read a failed SIP call? Start with the stage where the call stopped. The map below gives each stage a first check, and it's our own troubleshooting order rather than part of any standard. The first digit of a response code tells you who needs to act: Class Meaning Codes you'll meet 1xx Still working 100 Trying, 180 Ringing, 183 Session Progress 2xx Accepted 200 OK 3xx Try elsewhere 302 Moved Temporarily 4xx This request can't succeed as sent 401, 404, 407, 408, 480, 486, 487, 488 5xx The server failed 500, 503 6xx Nobody can accept this 600 Busy Everywhere, 603 Decline When a firewall rewrites SIP A firewall can change your SIP messages as well as filter them. Fortinet's FortiGate guide, for example, says its SIP session helper opens SIP and RTP pinholes and translates addresses inside SIP messages, and that SIP ALG mode adds further checks. If an SDP address or Contact header looks wrong, compare traces from both sides of the firewall. Change these settings only after that comparison shows the firewall is altering the messages. Which SIP transport should you use? RFC 3261 requires every SIP element to implement UDP and TCP. Its default ports are 5060 for UDP and TCP, and 5061 for TLS. Choose When Watch for TLS Signalling crosses the public internet Certificates and renewals TCP You stay on a private network and messages grow large Long-lived connections through NAT UDP You stay on a controlled network and need the simplest setup Fragmentation. RFC 3261 moves requests above about 1,300 bytes to a congestion-controlled transport when the path MTU is unknown WebSocket The client is a browser, under RFC 7118 Client and server must both support it What secures a SIP call? SIP security comes in separate layers, and each one protects a different thing: TLS protects signalling one hop at a time. RFC 3261 warns that using TLS to a proxy gives no assurance of TLS end to end. SRTP protects the audio. TLS doesn't encrypt RTP, so you must enable SRTP separately. A mismatch can leave a connected call silent. Digest authentication proves identity. It avoids sending the password itself, and RFC 8760 adds SHA-256 options to the original algorithm. Source controls and destination limits contain damage. The SIP trunking guide has a full hardening checklist. Do you need to handle SIP yourself? Often you don't. Use this map to choose how much of the protocol you take on, then compare SIP with WebSocket streaming if you're building for voice AI. Two neighbouring terms cause confusion here. VoIP is the wider category, and SIP is one protocol used within it, as SIP vs VoIP explains. WebRTC is a browser media stack, and it doesn't define which signalling you use. What should you know about SIP in India? SIP itself works the same in India, but the rules on what you signal are specific and active. The table connects each part of a call to its rule. Rules change often, so confirm the current text and take legal advice for your own case. Part of the call Rule Source and date Calling number, promotional Use the 140xx series after registering with your telecom provider TRAI press release 91/2026, July 2026 Calling number, service or transactional Entities regulated by RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, and PFRDA, plus government bodies, use the 1600xx series Calls started by software Declare A2P calls and their CLI ranges to your originating provider in advance. Undeclared calls count as unsolicited TRAI Third Amendment, September 2026 The trunk itself First unsolicited-call violation by a sender: outgoing services on all its telecom resources, including SIP trunks, barred for 15 days. Later violations: those resources disconnected for one year TCCCPR Second Amendment, February 2025, and restated in the Third Amendment Each number on the trunk For the restoration provisions, each DID on a PRI or SIP trunk counts as a separate resource Three points deserve attention if you build on SIP. Voice agents appear to fit the A2P definition. The Third Amendment covers calls started by an application, software system, or automated platform without direct human dialling, including artificial voice. An outbound voice agent seems to match that wording, so raise it with your provider before launch. Regulation 4 on declaration starts 60 days after Gazette publication. We could not confirm the publication date, so check whether it applies on your launch date. The name on the call is changing. Inc42 reports that DoT directed operators to roll out calling name presentation (CNAP) from November 1, 2026, on 4G and newer networks. It adds that business and bulk-connection users can display a preferred name backed by a registered trademark or GST trade name. We read this in a news report rather than the DoT order. The report doesn't mention SIP. CLI checks may tighten. TRAI has recommended CNAP for SIP and PRI calls reaching mobile networks, and a CLI authentication framework when providers extend SIP or PRI trunks to enterprises. These are recommendations, and we could not confirm how far each has been implemented. For toll bypass and more enforcement detail, see the India section of What is SIP trunking?. How Vobiz handles SIP Vobiz SIP trunking exposes the protocol where you need it and handles it where you don't.. Trunks. The console has separate pages for outbound and inbound trunks. The Trunks API sets each trunk's direction. The handshake's identity step. Attach an IP access control list or a SIP credential. Credential trunks are challenged with 407 Proxy Authentication Required. Transport and encryption. The trunk settings choose UDP, TCP, or TLS for signalling, and a separate setting controls SRTP for media. Paths. Signalling and media use different addresses, and media flows directly rather than through the signalling SBCs. Open the ranges on that page, because allowing only the SIP ports gives you a connected call with no audio. Endpoints. SIP endpoints register their own addresses. The API reports whether each endpoint is registered, its contact address, and when the registration expires, so you can check a binding directly. Transfers. SIP trunking supports blind and warm transfer through REFER, and the Transfer API works on a live call from your own code. No SIP at all. With VobizXML, your server returns call logic through webhooks (callbacks), and Vobiz handles the signalling. Audio Streams then fork live audio to your WebSocket server. Tracing a session on Vobiz The SIP call logs include a SIP Trace view of the raw messages with timing, the hangup cause code, and the authentication method used. Open a call and select the More tab to find them. The CDR API can filter by SIP Call-ID, which lets you match a Vobiz record to your own PBX trace. Each record also reports the negotiated codec, plus call-quality scores, jitter, and packet loss. The hangup causes reference explains each code and its next step. India on Vobiz Vobiz's India calling regulations cover KYC, caller ID, and media anchoring. Both legs of an Indian call must stay in India. A breach ends the call with hangup cause 2070, and a caller ID that isn't a Vobiz number ends it with 3030. See 140 and 160 series acquisition for commercial numbers and UCC management for complaints. Test calls are billed to your account. Run them with your own Auth ID and Auth Token, and confirm the numbers first. Current rates are on the Vobiz pricing page. Frequently asked questions FAQ In the protocol, a SIP session is the live media exchange between participants, created when the SDP offer and answer complete. In carrier quotes, the phrase can mean one concurrent call, the same capacity unit as a channel. Check which meaning applies before you compare plans. What is the SIP three-way handshake? It is the INVITE, 200 OK, and ACK exchange that establishes a call. The caller asks, the callee accepts, and the caller confirms that it received the acceptance. The third message exists because a person may take a long time to answer. How does a SIP session differ from a SIP dialog? The dialog is the signalling relationship, identified by the Call-ID and two tags. The session is the media that relationship controls. A dialog can exist while a phone rings, before any session starts, and a hold changes the session without creating a new dialog. It is a keepalive defined in RFC 4028. The two sides negotiate an interval with the Session-Expires header, then send a re-INVITE or UPDATE at about the halfway point. If no refresh arrives in time, each side treats the session as ended and should send BYE. What port does SIP use? The defaults are port 5060 for SIP over UDP or TCP, and port 5061 for SIP over TLS. Those ports carry signalling only. RTP audio uses separate ports chosen for each call and named in the SDP, so your firewall has to allow both. Is SIP the same as VoIP? No. VoIP is the broad category of carrying voice over IP networks. SIP is one signalling protocol used within it, and it handles call setup, changes, and teardown. A VoIP call that uses SIP still relies on RTP or SRTP to carry the audio. Further reading on Vobiz What is SIP trunking? · SIP vs VoIP · What is WebRTC? articles.title: No‑Up‑Front‑Cost Web Design Promises Fast Sites — SMBs weigh hidden fees versus instant launch
articles.description: No‑Up‑Front‑Cost Web Design Promises Fast Sites — SMBs weigh hidden fees versus instant launch Decision Context: Choosing a No‑Up‑Front‑Cost Web Design Model You run a small‑to‑mid‑size service business and need a professional website within weeks but you have limited cash to spend today. Several vendors promise a no‑up‑front‑cost site, yet the term hides three distinct delivery models that differ in cash‑flow impact, total cost of ownership, and code ownership. This guide walks you through the three common models, shows how to compare them with a concrete decision‑aid matrix, and outlines the practical steps to lock in a contract that protects your budget and future flexibility. 1. The Three Models Behind the “No‑Up‑Front‑Cost” Claim Model Cash outlay before any work Typical payment schedule When full ownership transfers Design engine Pay‑monthly AI‑augmented studio £0 (or $0) – you only sign a service agreement £50 × 12 ≈ £600 per year (example from a UK provider) After the final scheduled payment (month 12) you own the design, content, and code outright【S2】 ~90 % AI, 10 % human review Build‑first agency (traditional upfront) One lump‑sum deposit (often 30 % of total) or full fee before launch €299 (minimum) or higher, paid once on delivery【S2】 Immediately on receipt of final payment – you own everything from day 1 Human designers, optional AI tools Free‑setup service (no‑deposit) £0 – the provider builds a site at no charge for setup【S5】 Ongoing subscription (often $15–$30 / month) or modest maintenance fee Ownership is usually retained by the provider; you pay a usage fee to keep the site live【S5】 Varies – many rely on hosted builder platforms Only the pay‑monthly AI‑augmented studio hands over full ownership after you have completed the payment cycle. The other two give you a live site immediately, but you either keep paying a subscription or never own the underlying code. 2. Cash‑Flow Relief vs. Total Cost of Ownership Factor Pay‑monthly AI studio Build‑first agency Free‑setup service Initial cash needed £0 €299 (or higher) Year‑1 cash outlay £600 (12 × £50) €299 (one‑time) $180 – $360 (12 × $15‑$30) Projected 3‑year cash outlay £1 800 (assuming you stay the full term) €299 + possible redesign fees (≈ £1 200) $540 – $1 080 Ownership point Month 12 Day 1 Never (unless you migrate) Typical hidden fees Extra revisions after design freeze, premium plugins Redesign after 2–3 years, content migration Platform lock‑in, transaction fees for e‑commerce A pay‑monthly plan eases cash‑flow but can be more expensive over three years, especially if you cancel early. An upfront project demands a larger initial spend but often results in a lower total spend if you keep the site for several years and avoid recurring platform fees. Free‑setup services look cheap initially but the ongoing subscription can eclipse a modest upfront project after a year or two. 3. Who Owns the Site (and the Code)? Pay‑monthly AI studio – Ownership transfers only after the final scheduled payment. Until then the provider retains a licence to the code and may suspend the site if payments lapse【S2】. Build‑first agency – Contracts usually stipulate that the client receives all source files (HTML, CSS, assets) on delivery. The agency’s liability ends once the hand‑over is complete. Free‑setup service – The site lives on the provider’s hosted platform; you are granted a user account, not the underlying code. Moving the site elsewhere often incurs migration fees or requires rebuilding【S5】. If you anticipate needing full control—e.g., to add custom e‑commerce functionality, integrate a CRM, or switch hosts—ensure the contract explicitly states code ownership and right to export before you sign. 4. Design Quality & Performance: AI‑Heavy vs. Human‑Centric Studios Aspect AI‑heavy (≈90 % AI) Human‑centric (custom agency) Speed of delivery 1–2 weeks from brief to live URL【S2】 4–8 weeks (depends on scope) Design originality Template‑based layouts with AI‑generated variations; limited brand nuance Fully custom visual language, brand‑aligned UI SEO foundation Basic on‑page SEO auto‑filled by AI; may miss niche keyword opportunities SEO audit, structured data, content strategy built in Performance Often built on lightweight frameworks; generic code can bloat if many plugins are added later Optimised code, selective asset loading, performance testing Revision cycles Usually 1–2 minor tweaks after hand‑off; major changes may require a new payment Multiple design iterations baked into the contract (often 3–4 rounds) AI‑driven sites can be perfectly adequate for simple brochure‑type pages (e.g., a plumber’s contact page). For businesses that rely on organic search or need a distinctive brand experience, a human‑centric approach typically yields higher conversion potential, albeit at a higher price. 5. Risk Profile: Cancellation, Vendor Lock‑In, and Ongoing Fees Risk Early cancellation Free before design work begins; after that you may owe a termination fee or lose the work already done【S2】 Not applicable (project ends on delivery) You can cancel the subscription, but the site disappears unless you migrate (costly) Vendor lock‑in Code is proprietary until month 12; after that you can export, but migration may need developer help Minimal lock‑in if you own the code; may need to re‑host High lock‑in; platform‑specific features cannot be moved without rebuilding Unexpected fees Extra revisions, premium plugins, hosting upgrades Redesign after 2–3 years, content updates not covered Platform fees, transaction fees for e‑commerce, premium templates Performance guarantees Usually “best effort”; SLA may be limited to uptime Agency may offer performance guarantees as part of contract SLA tied to platform provider, not the design service If your business cannot tolerate service interruption, prioritize a model with clear ownership and minimal lock‑in. 6. When Each Model Makes Sense Situation Recommended model Rationale Cash‑strapped startup that needs a live site within days No cash outlay, rapid launch, ownership after a year if you stay Local service provider (plumber, trainer) with a static site Low ongoing cost, minimal technical maintenance, acceptable lock‑in Mid‑size boutique that relies on SEO and brand differentiation Upfront investment yields custom SEO‑ready design and full code ownership Business planning a 3‑year horizon and expects custom integrations Build‑first agency (or hybrid: upfront + optional AI‑assisted maintenance) Avoids cumulative subscription fees and ensures code extensibility 7. Decision‑Aid: 5‑Point Checklist & Quick‑Calc Spreadsheet Below is a printable matrix you can fill in for any vendor you are evaluating. Use the Quick‑Calc column to compute the effective 12‑month cost (including any known hidden fees). # Evaluation Criterion Your Target (Y/N or numeric) Vendor Score (✓/✗ or amount) Quick‑Calc (£/€/$) 1 Zero upfront cash Y ✓ if no payment required before design work begins 0 2 Total 12‑month cost ≤ £800 ≤ 800 Enter quoted total (e.g., £600) £600 3 Ownership transfer month ≤ 12 Enter month number (e.g., 12) — 4 Design process Prefer ≥ 30 % human input Enter % AI / % human (e.g., 90 % AI) 5 Cancellation fee after design No fee or ≤ £100 Enter fee amount (e.g., £0) How to use it List each vendor you are considering in a separate row. Fill the Vendor Score cells with the data you gather from their proposals. In the Quick‑Calc column, add any extra costs you know (e.g., premium plugin £50, migration fee £200). Apply a simple rule: Accept any vendor that meets all three “hard” targets (rows 1‑3) and scores at least 3‑out of 5 on the softer criteria (rows 4‑5). Example Vendor Decision Alpha Studio (pay‑monthly) ✓ 12 90 % AI ✗ (cancellation fee £150) Reject (fails row 5) Beta Agency (upfront) ✗ (requires £299 deposit) £299 0 % AI Reject (fails row 1) Gamma Platform (free‑setup) £240 (12 × $20) – (no ownership) 100 % platform Reject (fails row 3) Delta Design (hybrid) £750 (incl. £100 premium plugin) 6 40 % AI Accept (meets all hard targets, decent human input) Print this table, fill it out, and you’ll have a transparent basis for a contract decision. 8. Practical Next Steps Gather proposals from at least two providers in each model category. Populate the decision‑aid matrix using the exact figures from their contracts. Request a clause that guarantees a clean export of all source files (HTML, CSS, assets) at the ownership transfer point. Run a quick performance test on any demo URL they give you (e.g., Google PageSpeed Insights) to verify load times and mobile friendliness. Schedule a 30‑day trial (if offered) and evaluate the site’s ability to capture leads before committing to the full payment schedule. By following this structured approach you can avoid the common pitfall of “free‑now, costly‑later” and choose a web‑design model that aligns with both your cash‑flow constraints and long‑term growth ambitions. 9. Safety‑Sensitive Considerations If your website will host personal data, health information, or financial transactions, treat the design provider as a component of a broader compliance effort. Verify that: The provider’s hosting environment meets relevant security standards (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2). Any AI‑generated copy or code is reviewed by a qualified human before publishing. You retain the ability to disable the site instantly in case of a breach. A documented incident‑response plan exists that includes both the provider and your internal team. Next Action: Download the checklist table above, list three local vendors (one from each model), and fill in the matrix by Friday. Use the completed matrix to negotiate contract terms that include code export rights and a clear cancellation policy. articles.title: How to Register a Company in Pakistan for a Digital Marketing Agency
articles.description: I’ll be honest, I put this off for almost a year. My agency was already taking on clients, invoicing them, and doing the work—just without any legal backbone. Then a client in Dubai asked for an incorporation certificate before releasing a $2,000 payment, and I had nothing to show him. That was the push I needed to actually register my company in Pakistan instead of quietly hoping nobody would ask. What I want to share here isn’t a copy-paste checklist on how to register a company in Pakistan. It’s what genuinely happened when I sat down with the SECP portal open, my CNIC scanned on my phone, and no real idea what I was doing. Why Bother to Register a Company in Pakistan at All? If you’re doing small local work, you can get away with being unregistered for a while. I did, for over a year. But the second you want a proper business bank account, or you want to use Payoneer under a company name instead of your personal one, people start asking for paperwork you don’t have. I actually lost a project worth around $600 because their finance department wanted an SECP certificate and a company NTN, not just a freelancing profile screenshot. That stung enough that I finally decided to register my company in Pakistan the right way. Picking a Structure: Single Member Company (SMC) vs. Private Limited Before you can properly register a company in Pakistan, you need to pick a business structure. SECP gives you a few routes. Sole proprietorship isn’t strictly an SECP process—that is handled through FBR. The two main options that matter if you want to formally incorporate are: Single Member Company (SMC-Private Limited): Ideal if you are a solo owner. You are still treated as a private limited company legally, which provides corporate status while allowing full ownership. Private Limited Company (Pvt Ltd): Better if you have co-founders or plan to bring in investors early, since shares are split between two or more directors from day one. My advice: If it’s just you starting out, don’t overcomplicate it—go with an SMC. You can always convert it into a multi-member Private Limited setup later as your team and equity structure grow. Step-by-Step SECP eServices Filing Process Here is the exact order of steps I followed on the SECP eServices portal (eservices.secp.gov.pk): 1. Name Reservation You submit up to three name options in order of preference. My top choice was approved the next working day. Make sure your proposed business name is unique and does not violate trademark guidelines to avoid rejections. 2. Memorandum and Articles of Association (MOA & AOA) This is where many first-time founders hit a roadblock. SECP provides standardized objective clauses for recognized sectors. Selecting "digital marketing and advertising services" from the pre-approved list speeds up processing. If your business objective is vaguely worded, expect review queries and delays. 3. Document Submission You will need to upload: Scanned copies of your CNIC (front and back). Passport-sized photograph. Proof of registered business address (such as a lease agreement or utility bill). Signed MOA and AOA pages. 4. Fee Payment For a basic authorized capital structure, fees are processed online via 1Link or credit card. Keep your initial authorized capital at a realistic baseline, as higher authorized capital directly increases the SECP registration fee. 5. Issuance of Incorporation Certificate Within a few working days of approval, SECP issues a digitally signed Certificate of Incorporation via email. This document officially confirms your corporate existence. Common Pitfalls to Avoid If I had to go through the incorporation process again, here is what I would do differently: Separate SECP and FBR Registrations: SECP incorporation gives you legal company status, but you must separately register your corporate National Tax Number (NTN) through the FBR IRIS portal to become tax compliant. Registered Office Address Selection: Avoid using a temporary residential address if you plan to move offices soon. Changing your official registered address later requires statutory filing with SECP. Annual Compliance Requirements: Even if your agency declares minimal or zero revenue in its initial months, SECP mandates annual statutory filings (such as Form A/29). Stay ahead of compliance deadlines to avoid late surcharge notices. Operational Advantages Post-Registration Incorporating the agency delivered immediate operational benefits: Corporate Banking: Enabled opening a dedicated corporate bank account with local banks like Bank Alfalah or Meezan Bank. International Payment Gateways: Allowed setup of a verified Payoneer business account for international client billing. Enterprise Credibility: Eliminates friction when pitching corporate clients, signing non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), and issuing formal commercial proposals. Summary of Estimated Costs SECP Filing & Incorporation Fee: PKR 1,500 – 5,000 (varies by authorized capital) Corporate NTN Registration (FBR): Free Legal / Consultant Assistance (Optional): PKR 8,000 – 15,000 Total Estimated DIY Setup Cost: Under PKR 5,000 Final Thoughts If you are currently running your agency informally, don't wait for a payment blockage or a missed contract to force your hand. The SECP digital filing workflow is straightforward once your documentation is organized. Are you currently navigating SECP incorporation or FBR setup for your agency? Feel free to leave your questions in the comments section below! Published by Media Initiation — Digital Marketing & Web Architecture Specialists.

articles.title: Four Evenings, One Walking Atlas: AI Agents Are Not Just for Coding
articles.description: How a static BattleTech board game got animated mechs — without me becoming an artist (and avoiding "AI slop" as much as possible). A few readers of this blog will know that in my spare time I'm building my own digital version of BattleTech known as MakaMek. And usually that's the only topic I'm motivated enough to write about. But I haven't posted anything in a while. They say that "coding is solved" so why should I even bother? 😄 At the same time you always want to have some fun, if coding is no fun anymore — the solution is to look somewhere else. One of the features I have wanted for MakaMek for as long as the project has existed is unit animations. So is it possible for me to become an artist? The art is the weakest part of any app I have ever made. With MakaMek I was lucky enough as another (much older and bigger) implementation of BattleTech — MegaMek — was around for decades. Dozens of contributors added thousands of unit assets — literally everything you can think of in the universe. I leverage this effort by using MegaMek's artwork in my game. But a unit in MegaMek is a single 84×72 top-down image. Functional, readable, and completely unusable as a source for animation. You can't rig a PNG. Or you can try with AI, but AI-generated sprites are not something I wanted to do. I needed a proper deterministic pipeline that would allow me to reliably produce the same sprites every time I run it. And the AI could have a boring part of the job — to babysit the pipeline while it runs. An old trick So I remembered something obvious: games have been faking 3D with 2D sprites for decades. MechCommander, one of the first BattleTech games I played, did exactly this in the late 90s. The mechs were 3D models rendered from fixed angles and turned into sprites. They looked heavy and believable because the silhouette came from a real model. And to be honest I did exactly the same thing somewhere in 2007 with "white" and "blue" dice for Magical Yatzy. So yes, rendering 3D models into 2D sprites is an old technique, but you need a source of 3D models — and a way to automate the process, otherwise rendering even a tiny fraction of units I support currently would take forever. The source Piranha Games has been producing BattleTech units since MechWarrior Online, and those designs are now part of the visual vocabulary of the franchise. They show up in MechWarrior 5, in HBS's BattleTech, and in multiple fan-made animations like Hired Steel (I really recommend this one by the way). Whatever you think of the games, the models are excellent: detailed, consistent, and instantly recognizable (thank you @Flyingdebris). But the important part for automation is the structure. MW5's assets are named consistently and organized with a proper machine-readable structure in Unreal Engine packages. Mods extend the same structure with more units. The only problem is that I've never worked with Unreal Engine and had no idea how all that stuff works, but that was exactly the part I was ready to delegate to AI. Evening one: the render that didn't look right I started with one deliberately small question: can a single MW5 Atlas, exported by hand (I used an open-source app called FModel) and rendered headlessly in Blender at board size, look comparable to the current MegaMek art? The answer was no. At least not at first. The first 84×72 render was a gray, busy mass. It read as "some mech" but was almost indistinguishable from noise: the model's panel lines and greebles were smaller than a pixel. And the head was missing entirely, apparently in MW5 the cockpit is a separate mesh as well as all the weapon systems and equipment. MegaMek's hand-drawn sprite had more personality and was way more recognizable. I kept playing with it and came up with a few improvements that worked: render at 4× and downsample, real antialiasing, a clean one-pixel outline. I also stopped rendering at fixed 84×72 size (MegaMek legacy), each mech should get a canvas fitted to its own silhouette. Behind those fixes was a decision not to build a custom renderer. Blender (another tool I've never touched) does the rendering; the pipeline only drives it. That kept the experiment small enough to finish in one evening. I tested the final rendering script on a second unit — the Annihilator. That second image also gave me a useful surprise: the pipeline isn't uniformly good or bad. The Atlas is close to a worst case — broad shoulders, arms held wide, little depth. The Annihilator reads much better from directly above because its plan view is deeper. Readability is chassis-dependent, which means the pipeline probably needs a review pass on different models. Evening two: teaching the agent to open the box Hand-exporting one (or eventually two) mech skeletons is one thing, but hand-exporting hundreds of fully assembled variants is a lifestyle choice I wasn't ready to make. So the next question was: can the agent read the game's pak files itself? MW5 runs on Unreal Engine 4.26. Its assets live in a 100 GiB pak with 285,997 virtual files. The agent built a small C# tool on top of CUE4Parse, the open-source library behind FModel, and started exploring. By the end of the task it could mount the game, enumerate all the chassis, classify every body, cockpit, glass and weapon mesh, and dump the custom hardpoint and loadout data. The tool read the loadout, followed the weapon tag, found the hardpoint visual, and placed the mesh on the right bone. AS7-D came out with an AC/20, LRM20, SRM6 and medium lasers. AS7-RS, same chassis, came out with an AC/10, LRM15, SRM4 and large lasers. Visibly different and "canon" correct at the same time. That was the moment the project stopped being a rendering experiment and became an asset pipeline. The agent used CUE4Parse to read the pak, Blender to render previews and final frames, Python scripts to inspect meshes, and later SharpGLTF to write animation because CUE4Parse can't export animated glTF. It picked tools the way a person would: whatever gets the job done and can be checked. Evening three: making it walk Static mechs are nice. Walking mechs were the whole point of starting this adventure. Animations turned out to be their own little archaeology project. The body mesh and the animations are separate assets in MW5 models. Bone indices don't line up between the shared skeleton, the chassis mesh and the clip, so everything has to be mapped by name. The walk clip translates the root by 8.6 meters even though the file says root motion is locked. The source is 30 fps with 61 keys for a two-second loop, and the closing key duplicates the first pose. The agent found all of this by probing the data in the pak. Then it did the unglamorous part: sample the loop at 12 fps, strip the root motion, render ten frames, pack them into a spritesheet, and build a gif file so I could review the whole cycle in one image instead of opening ten PNGs. The result reads as walking. Not because the legs move a lot — from directly above, a forward step is barely visible — but because the feet alternate and the body shifts its weight by about five pixels. That's enough. The eye fills in the rest. Unfortunately I couldn't get everything I wanted and needed for MakaMek: MW5 never shipped knockdown, so there are no prone or stand-up animations to extract. I'll decide what to do with it later, but even if I don't — it still would be better than it was. Evening four: putting it on the board The last evening was integration into the game. MakaMek's unit packages are zip files with a manifest, a JSON definition and a PNG. I extended the format additively: v1 packages behave exactly as before, v2 packages can carry an optional spritesheet and metadata. If the spritesheet is missing or broken, the unit falls back to its static image. No unit ever disappears because an animation failed. On the runtime side, a received move command now plays over a fixed five seconds (will be configurable or disabled via settings). Position, facing and sprite frame share one linear clock. The frame is driven by distance traveled, not time, so the feet stay planted at any speed. And yes, the first in-game version had the mech walking backwards. The model's forward axis and the board's facing convention disagreed by 180°. One re-render later it was fixed. What the agent actually did I want to be precise about this, because the hype version of this story is misleading. The agent did not have the idea. It did not decide that the Atlas should read as a heavy mech, that the outline should be one pixel, or that a five-second move feels right. It did not look at the first render and say, "the head is missing, and that matters." What it did was carry the work. It read unfamiliar APIs, wrote the extractor, the Blender driver, the spritesheet packer, the package reader, the playback timeline and the tests. It ran renders, measured the results, compared frames, and wrote the docs. It kept going when the eleventh API call failed. It did in an evening (while I was cooking dinner) what would have taken me weeks of context switching, Blender tutorials and swearing. I brought taste, context and acceptance criteria. The agent brought patience, recall and throughput. The workflow that made it work was simple: every step had to produce something I could look at — a render, a contact sheet, a JSON report, a diff. The agent could explore freely as long as it came back with evidence. The honest limits Licensing. MW5 models and renders derived from them are PGI/Microsoft IP. The tooling can ship; the art cannot. Everything I rendered lives in a gitignored folder and is loaded as a local asset pack. Coverage. This is one chassis, end to end. MW5 has 104 chassis; MakaMek has 199 variants. Batch rendering is a matter of hours, but reviewing the output is still human work. Missing animation. Prone, stand-up and idle breathing don't exist in the source. They need to be authored, not just extracted. The agent is confidently wrong sometimes. It once scaled the outline thickness twice and turned a 4× render into a black blob. The lesson is the same as with code: look at the output. Why this is bigger than my hex map The interesting part of this project isn't that an AI wrote some C#. It's that the same loop applies to almost any task, including ones you would never call software development. An agent is not a code generator with a chat window. It's a process executor that happens to be very good at code. The loop looks like this: Find a source of truth. Build a small tool to read it. Visualize the result. Compare it to what you wanted. Fix the gap. Automate the repeat. That loop is not coding. It's how you get anything done in an unfamiliar domain. The takeaway Four evenings. One walking Atlas. A pipeline that can, in principle, do this for every mech I can legally render. Would I have done it by hand? Maybe. In a few months, with a lot of Blender tutorials and a lot of swearing. That's the real productivity gain. Not ten times more code per hour — a lower barrier to starting something you don't know how to do yet. Next: the other 198 variants, authored prone and stand-up clips, an idle that breathes, and a Locust that doesn't look like a coffee table. Behind the scenes The whole thing is documented in the open, including the dead ends: #1642 — first render, static Atlas #1652 — headless extraction and assembled variants #1653 — animation clips and spritesheets #1659 — mmux v2 and in-game playback The pipeline, in one line: MW5 pak → MW5Extractor → assembled glTF → headless Blender → spritesheet → .mmux v2 → UnitControl If you want the technical version, the design and the extraction notes are in the repo under docs/architecture/asset-pipeline.md, docs/architecture/blender-render-driver.md and docs/analysis/mw5-model-extraction.md.

articles.title: Writing a review-ready PR body from a short diff, no install required
articles.description: My pull request descriptions used to be two words and a shrug. "fixes stuff", "cleanup", sometimes nothing at all. Then I would watch a reviewer spend the first ten minutes of a review reconstructing what the change was for, which is work I had already done in my head and failed to write down. The code was usually fine; the missing context was the bottleneck. The fix was not more discipline. It was a template that asked me the questions a reviewer always asks anyway, and a way to fill it from the diff I already had. Four headings: Summary, What changed, How to test, Notes. That is it. Once the shape exists, I stop staring at an empty textarea. The four headings a reviewer actually reads Summary is one or two sentences of intent, not a restatement of the diff. "Make the retry path idempotent so a duplicate webhook cannot create a second order" tells a reviewer what to check; "changes retry.py" does not. What changed is the short mechanical list: which modules, which behaviour, whether anything is deliberately out of scope. I want this separate from the intent, because a reviewer compares the two and the interesting bugs live in the gap between them. How to test is the section that earns its keep. Exact commands, the state to set up, the edge case to try, what "correct" looks like. When I leave it blank, a reviewer either guesses or asks, and both cost a round trip. Notes is where the awkward stuff goes: a migration that needs a follow-up, a flag that is off by default, a known limitation, a decision I want someone to push back on. Putting it in writing means it survives the merge instead of living in a thread nobody reopens. PrGen turns commits or a short diff into exactly that structure: a structured PR body with Summary, What changed, How to test, and Notes, review-ready as a draft. No installation, no repo permissions, nothing to configure. Why no GitHub App is a real design decision The feature I am most asked about is a GitHub App, and the answer is no, on purpose. An App would pull the branch, the linked issues, the CI status, and the file list without me pasting anything. It would also need an OAuth grant, a permission scope, a place to run, and a security review before anyone on the team could install it. For a tool whose whole job is producing a paragraph of text, that is a lot of machinery and a lot of trust. The cost is real and I will not pretend otherwise. No App means no automatic issue linking, no branch name, no CI result, no diff stats pulled on my behalf. If I want those in the body, I type them. Nothing syncs, nothing updates when I push another commit, and the tool has no idea a PR exists after I close the tab. This is a trade-off, not a victory lap: I am trading automatic context for a smaller trust surface and zero setup. The test notes are still mine to verify Here is the honest limit. The PR body is a draft, and the "How to test" section is the part most likely to be confidently wrong if I stop paying attention. A generated set of steps can describe the happy path and miss the one state that actually breaks: an existing user with a null field, a clock skewed by a day, a feature flag half-rolled-out. Those come from knowledge of the system, not from the diff. So I read the draft, correct the test steps against what I actually ran, and confirm the Notes section does not claim a decision the team has not made. A reviewer should treat the body as a starting point, not as evidence the change was verified. It is decision-support for writing the description, not a live audit of the branch, a review approval, or a certification that the change is safe. The sign-off still belongs to a human who ran the code. If your PR descriptions are still a blank box and a silent prayer, pasting a commit range into PrGen and editing the resulting four sections is a five-minute change that moves the review conversation forward. Then do the part it cannot: run the steps and mean them. FAQ Does it open the PR or post to GitHub for me? No. It produces a structured PR body from what you paste. It does not open PRs, post comments, read GitHub, or check CI. There is no App to install. Is the generated How to test section verified? No. It is a draft. Confirm the steps against what you actually ran; a reviewer's sign-off still belongs to a human. Why no GitHub App? Fewer permissions and zero setup, at the cost of no automatic issue linking, branch context, or CI status. It is decision-support, not a live audit of your branch.
