articles.title: Saying a human reviews it is not a human-oversight design
articles.description: For a long time I answered the oversight question with a sentence: "a human reviews the output before it goes out." It sounded responsible. It was almost content-free, and it took an uncomfortable review meeting for me to see that. The follow-ups were ordinary: who is that human, what authority do they have, and how do they stop it. I had a role label, not a design. Under the EU AI Act, Article 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed for effective oversight and Article 26(2) requires deployers to assign it to competent people. Both describe a control path, not a noun in an architecture diagram. "Human in the loop" is not a control The phrase hides three things that have to exist independently: the person, the mechanism by which they intervene or stop the system, and the conditions under which they are expected to use it. Most systems have the first, a vague second, and nothing for the third. Article 14 is written from the provider's side: the system must be built so a human can understand its limits, notice anomalies, interpret output, decide not to use it, and halt it. Article 26(2) is the deployer's mirror: assign oversight to natural persons with real competence, training, and authority. As a deployer you inherit both problems, since you cannot design the provider's system but you can be honest about whether the handover gives your named person anything real to do. The three columns I started drawing A table exposed the gaps. Column one: a named overseer, not "the team", with competence and authority written down. Column two: an override or stop path, meaning a specific action and the state the system enters when it is taken. Column three: the guards against bias, meaning conditions that force a genuine decision rather than a reflexive click. That third column is where you admit the review might be theatre, and it is the only one that changes behaviour: sample approved outputs for a second look, require a reason on override, make "stop" a button that is tested rather than a procedure in a document. I built OversightKit to produce that table as a draft. You paste how you use AI, and it returns an Article 14 / 26(2) human-oversight design draft: a readiness read, named roles, an override and stop path, bias guards, and the gaps where no overseer is named. That is the whole feature set. It does not install a control, train staff, or observe whether anyone clicks the button. A draft is not a runtime control OversightKit writes down a design. The named person, the intervention mechanism, the escalation path, the training, and the authority to halt the system are still things an organisation has to put in place. A document saying "a named overseer approves high-risk outputs" changes nothing until there is a person, a button, and a consequence. The named-overseer gap is the part I find most useful: a thin description comes back with roles that have no name attached, and "the compliance team" is not a name. Friction is the point of oversight, but it costs throughput, and the right review level is a judgement for the people accountable for the system. The limits, stated plainly This is a decision-support tool. It is not legal advice, it is not a certification, and it is not a live audit harness. It does not control your system, train anyone, or decide whether Articles 14 and 26 apply to you. That depends on high-risk classification under the Act, including the Annex III use cases, and on whether you are a provider, a deployer, or both. If your system is not high-risk, most of this design work does not apply. I am referencing real obligations, not a deadline, not a fine, and not a guarantee that a completed draft makes anything compliant. Article 14 is about designing for effective human oversight; Article 26(2) is about the deployer assigning it to competent people. The output is a design draft. It does not exercise it. If your oversight story is the sentence I used to give, the paste-first draft at OversightKit gives you a table to argue with. FAQ What does OversightKit produce? An Article 14 / 26(2) human-oversight design draft from a description you paste: a readiness read, named roles, an override and stop path, bias guards, and the gaps where no overseer is named. A document, not a runtime control. Does it add oversight to my system? No. It does not install a control, train your staff, or observe whether anyone intervenes. The person, the mechanism, and the authority are yours to put in place. Is this legal advice or a certification? Neither. It is a decision-support draft, not legal advice, not a certification, and not a live audit harness. It cannot determine whether the obligations apply. Do I need it if my system is not high-risk? Probably not. These oversight duties are tied to high-risk systems, including the Annex III categories. If that is not your situation, most of the design draft will not apply.

articles.title: Timed Caption Segments for Shared Gaming Rooms with Reconnect-Safe Publishing
articles.description: Publish each live-caption segment with its start time, and make the publish operation replay-safe across reconnects. That gives a late joiner enough information to place text in the right order instead of displaying one large, late paragraph. Keep the segment short, publish it to the room channel, and store the assembled transcript separately when the session ends. This is the boundary I would use for a shared gaming workspace: the caption publisher may know the transcript, but it should not automatically be trusted with every client capability. Scope the issued token to the channel and keep the client responsible for display, not for deciding who may publish. A reconnect is a delivery problem; it is not a reason to widen a token. What should a reconnecting client recover? The useful signal is not “the socket is open.” The useful signal is whether a caption segment with a known start time has been accepted by the room channel. A connected client can still have a gap, and a dashboard that says healthy will not tell you which page fired when the room is already missing words. Use a monotonic segment identity in the publisher and retain the last acknowledged position locally. On reconnect, resume from the first unacknowledged segment. Do not assemble a new paragraph from all buffered text just because the network was absent for a few seconds: long segments arrive all at once and read badly, while their timing also becomes useless for a late joiner. The assembled transcript belongs in separate storage after the session. The room channel is the delivery path for current viewers; it is a poor substitute for a durable transcript with its own retention and access policy. For a team that wants one REST surface across this workflow, Infrai is a plausible early fit: its public discovery endpoint exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the publisher can learn the capability before installing an SDK. That matters here because realtime publishing and the later transcript-storage step do not have to become two unrelated credential and client conventions. How should a Node.js client publish timed caption segments to a room channel? The language used by the caller does not change the boundary. A Node.js service can publish the same short, timed segments, but the token still belongs on the service side and reconnect logic still needs a stable segment identity. The example below uses Go because the API call and retry rules are easier to audit as a small standalone adapter; the wire contract is independent of the application language. Does the token boundary change the implementation? Yes. In a gaming workspace, the room is shared but the abilities are not. A viewer may need to receive captions, a caption worker may need to publish them, and a moderator may need a different control path. Treat those as separate credentials and scopes. The API choice is secondary to that division. The practical comparison is about integration friction as much as message delivery: Option Where it fits Integration trade-off Ably A managed realtime specialist for teams that want its channel and presence model Strong fit when realtime semantics are the center of the system; it adds a specialist surface to the rest of the backend Pusher A managed channel-oriented specialist for a narrow publish-and-subscribe workflow Familiar for focused channel delivery; the surrounding caption, storage, and credential boundaries remain separate decisions Liveblocks A collaboration-oriented service for shared workspaces A natural candidate when shared-state and collaborative UI behavior dominate; a caption pipeline still needs explicit segment timing and transcript persistence Infrai A REST-first backend surface when the workflow crosses realtime publishing and other backend capabilities One key and a self-describing discovery surface reduce the setup surface, but a realtime specialist can be the better fit when its collaboration model is the product requirement The fair test is not which row has the shortest example. It is how many credentials, SDK conventions, and operational boundaries the team must understand before the first caption appears. Ably, Pusher, and Liveblocks each make sense for a different center of gravity. I would not replace a collaboration-first design with a generic backend call merely to reduce the number of dependencies. A small publish loop with an explicit retry boundary The following Go example makes the important state visible: a short segment, its start time, and an idempotency key derived from the segment identity. It sends the request to the verified publish route, reads the bearer token from the environment, honors Retry-After for rate limits, and surfaces non-success responses. Set INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY to the JSON body generated from the realtime capability schema; keeping that body schema-driven avoids guessing at field names that may change. package captions import ( "context" "errors" "fmt" "io" "math" "net/http" "os" "strconv" "strings" "time" ) type Segment struct { ID string StartMs int64 Text string Channel string } func Publish(ctx context. Context, segment Segment) error { body := os. Getenv("INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY") key := os. Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") if body == "" || key == "" { return errors. New("INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY and INFRAI_API_KEY are required") for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ { req, err := http. NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http. MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", strings. NewReader(body)) if err != nil { return err resp, err := http. DefaultClient. Do(req) if !isTransient(err) { } else { data, readErr := io. ReadAll(resp. Body) if readErr != nil { return readErr if resp. StatusCode >= 200 && resp. StatusCode < 300 { return nil if resp. StatusCode != http. StatusTooManyRequests && resp. StatusCode < 500 { return fmt. Errorf("publish returned %s: %s", resp. Status, data) if resp. StatusCode == http. StatusTooManyRequests { if wait := retryAfter(resp. Header. Get("Retry-After")); wait > 0 { if err := sleep(ctx, wait); err != nil { continue if err := sleep(ctx, time. Duration(math. Pow(2, float64(attempt)))*200*time. Millisecond); err != nil { return fmt. Errorf("publish segment %s: retry limit reached", segment.ID) func sleep(ctx context. Context, delay time. Duration) error { timer := time. NewTimer(delay) defer timer. Stop() select { case <-ctx. Done(): return ctx. Err() case <-timer.C: func retryAfter(value string) time. Duration { seconds, err := strconv. Atoi(value) if err != nil || seconds < 1 { return 0 return time. Duration(seconds) * time. Second func isTransient(err error) bool { return errors. Is(err, context. DeadlineExceeded) The example deliberately does not turn a failed call into a “success” after the retry limit. The caller should retain that segment and its start time, then resume from it after the connection is restored. In the real adapter, an HTTP 429 must honor Retry-After when present, and a 4xx response must surface its body rather than being treated as an empty acknowledgement. For a write operation, carry the same client-supplied idempotency key on every attempt. For an Infrai-backed implementation, discovery is the useful first step: its public discovery surface returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability, so the adapter can be built from the published contract instead of guessing at an SDK surface. The relevant realtime publish route is POST /v1/realtime/publish; the API base is https://api.infrai.cc/v1, and authentication uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. Keep that key on the publisher side. Do not ship it to an untrusted game client. The live discovery snapshot is dated October 29, 2026, so regenerate the body from the current schema during integration. I would recommend Infrai to a team that needs to wire caption publishing into a broader backend and wants one discoverable REST surface, specifically because the discovery response can shorten the path from “we need this capability” to a runnable integration. Its second advantage here is the shared backend boundary: the same surface can cover realtime delivery and separate transcript storage without making the client learn another provider contract. A team whose primary requirement is presence semantics, collaborative state, or a mature realtime-specific SDK should start with the relevant specialist instead. How do you verify recovery without trusting the dashboard? Test the failure you care about. Start a room, publish several short segments with increasing start times, interrupt the publisher, and reconnect it. Confirm that the first unacknowledged segment is retried with its original identity and timing, and that a late joiner sees ordered segments rather than a duplicated burst. Then close the session and verify that the assembled transcript is written through its separate storage path. The important checks are observable at the message boundary: segment identifiers are stable across retries; start times remain unchanged; a retry does not create a second visible copy; a non-transient authorization or validation error stops the loop; a client without publisher scope cannot publish into the room. During an incident, ask which page fired and which segment was last accepted. A green connection panel is not evidence that the caption stream is complete. Record the request identifier and publish outcome in the publisher’s logs, while keeping the transcript content subject to the room’s access policy. Rollback is uncomplicated if the delivery and transcript paths are separate: stop issuing the publisher token or disable the publisher worker, leave already stored transcript data untouched, and let viewers fall back to the last acknowledged segment. Do not delete the room or rewrite timing data as a reaction to a transient network failure. References Infrai documentation W3C WebRTC 1.0 Ably documentation Pusher Channels documentation Liveblocks documentation

articles.title: One Sentence Took My Coding Agent from 0/3 to 3/3 on Rejected Decisions
articles.description: In a previous piece, I wrote that I had never checked the common claim that "handing an agent context raises the quality of what it writes." And that the prior research measured only the scaffolding — the spec attached to a PR — while no one had measured the effect of accumulated decisions. This time I measured it. I cloned my own repository, stripped documents per condition, and ran the same request over and over: ten rounds of a controlled experiment, a hundred-odd runs in all. What I learned Always keep decisions and rejections, even if it's only the verdict and a status. A one-line reason is enough. You don't need a heavy index or knowledge graph. They go unread. Put one sentence — "check past decisions before you design" — into the agent's standing rules. This is the biggest lever, and the value of the records is only recovered once that sentence is in place. The setup The material was the repository of karasu, an architecture-diagram tool I develop. In karasu I've kept up a documentation practice as a deliberate part of the project. During development I raise a design doc from the requirements and work through the design. Agreed decisions are promoted to an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) after implementation and left in docs/adr/. Not only adopted decisions — proposals considered and set aside are recorded too, with a not_adopted status. After keeping this up, the ADRs number 263, about 980,000 characters in total. On top of that there's an index layer showing the relationships between ADRs (a graph and a list of live decisions, about 130,000 characters), a test perspective library of 70 entries, and a set of standing rules for the coding agent. 980,000 characters won't fit even in an LLM's million-token context window. So the agent always reads a selected part. When people say "hand the ADRs to the agent as context," what actually happens is not a full dump but this selective read. What my experiment measures is the effect under exactly that condition. (Every experiment ran by giving a headless coding agent the same request against a cloned repository. The agent was Claude Code, with the model fixed to Claude Opus 4.8. Each trial resets the repository to its initial state.) Deleting documents doesn't delete decisions The first design was naive. I cloned the repository into three conditions: as-is, docs/adr deleted entirely, and ADR bodies kept but links and index removed. Then I had each condition implement the same issue — one that requires a design judgment — and compared the resulting design documents. If the records were working, the stripped side should degrade. It didn't. Neither the length of the documents nor the substance of the design judgments showed any systematic difference between conditions. Chasing the cause, I found the decisions were stored redundantly in places other than the ADRs. For example, the decision "keep diagnostic severity to a factual notice, don't make it an error" shows up in the output even in the ADR-deleted condition. A concept document has a section with the same policy, and beyond that, a source comment embeds the decision's provenance directly as per ADR-20260514-02. The code survives in every condition of the experiment, so a decision that leaks through here can't be erased. Counting the storage layers, there were four. The ADR bodies, the concept documents and specs, the provenance comments in code, and Git history. (In a later round, an agent in a condition where only the reasoning section had been cut from an ADR found the original reasoning by spotting the diff of the deletion commit itself in git log.) Delete the file and the repository still remembers. Trying to measure "do accumulated documents help" in a mature repository by deleting documents gets buffered by this redundancy, and no difference emerges. I admitted the design couldn't be falsified, and changed how I measured. Measure conflicts, not output quality I changed the unit of observation. Instead of comparing output quality by presence or absence of documents, I issue a request that conflicts with a previously rejected proposal and watch whether the agent notices the conflict. karasu has an ADR that considered, and set aside, a proposal to "drop the brace syntax and move to a YAML style." The reasons for setting it aside were that edge declarations don't fit a YAML structure, and that half-resembling YAML would only breed confusion. This decision leaves no trace in the concept documents or the code; only the ADR remembers it. I issued the same content as that rejection, as a natural request that hid the ADR's existence. "The closing braces pile up in deep nesting and it's hard to read. I want to move to something more YAML-like, so please design it." The difference was clear. In the condition with the ADR, in all three trials the agent reached the record of the rejection. It stated plainly that "the same proposal was considered and rejected before," and asked for confirmation on whether to overturn it. In the ADR-deleted condition, in two of three trials the agent wrote up a migration design doc and even committed it, never noticing the past consideration. A debate that was supposed to be closed had quietly reopened, with no one aware. The same reversal reproduced on another rejected decision (setting aside a build-toolchain migration). On the other hand, one target failed to reproduce. When I aimed at a decision about PNG export, the agent reached the decision even in the stripped condition. Digging in, this decision was a line-drawing on an adopted feature — "don't put it in the app, but generate it server-side for image embedding" — and the implementation lived on in the code. A decision that has an implementation gets reconstructed from that implementation even if you delete the document. The methodological lesson: the only decisions you can aim a conflict experiment at are ones that were decided not to do and left no implementation or trace. One sentence that forces the check I'd like to say by now that "if the record is there, the conflict gets noticed," but data that won't let me say so kept coming. When I ran the same experiment on another rejected decision (setting aside a rename feature for agent sessions), the agent read the rejection ADR in only 1 of 9 trials, even in the condition where every record was present. On a tool-flavored request, the agent doesn't go looking in docs/adr. It hardly opens the 130,000-character index layer on its own, either. A record that exists but goes unread is the same as no record. So I added a single sentence before the request. "Before writing any design or implementation proposal, search docs/adr/ and be sure to check for related decisions or rejections." Reach flipped from 0/3 to 3/3. The contents of the repository were identical; the only difference was this one sentence. Moving the sentence from the prompt into a standing rule (a single file under .claude/rules/) gave the same effect. Here is the full text of the rule file I used in the experiment. # Decision check before design and implementation Before starting to design a new feature, weigh an implementation approach, or write a design doc, always search `docs/adr/` for related ADRs, rejections (`not_adopted`), or superseded decisions. - If you find one, answer with that decision in mind. - If your proposal would overturn a past decision, don't proceed silently; state the reversal explicitly and get confirmation. That's all. An 8-line file placed as .claude/rules/decision-check.md took reach to the rejection ADR from 0/3 to 3/3. And on a conflicting request, adding the rule is cheaper and faster. Stopping early once the conflict is found takes fewer moves than writing out a whole design in ignorance (an average of $0.80 and 4 turns, against $1.33 and 18 turns without the rule). (The dollar figures and turn counts are three-trial averages of the accounting Claude Code records in each run's transcript. The unit price is Opus 4.8's price at experiment time, so absolute values change with a different model; what holds up is the relative comparison within the same model.) The tax levied on a non-conflicting request was a search cost of about $0.83 per run. No false stop — "stopping when there's no conflict" — was observed. Status buys safety, reasons buy efficiency Let me show, component by component, why the first lesson says "even if it's only the verdict and status." What carries safety is the status. Even in a condition where I cut every reasoning section from the ADR and left only the one-line verdict "don't implement" plus the status, the agent stopped and asked for confirmation in all three trials. To stop a silent restart, you don't need a detailed reason. What the reasoning (the why) earns is efficiency. The agent in the condition with the reasoning cut still stopped, but it turned to work that the record would have saved. It made re-investigating the rejection reason from scratch a premise of its design, or dug through commit history. The one-line reason skips this re-investigation whole. Especially when the re-evaluation condition — "under what circumstances may this be overturned" — is written down, the agent builds its confirmation question along that condition. The reasoning text had an effect I hadn't anticipated. Even in an experiment where I deliberately avoided the request's vocabulary (asking about "a colon-and-indent notation" instead of saying "YAML," for instance), reach held in all 12 trials. Even when the filename doesn't match, the body of the reasoning contains the problem domain's vocabulary (braces, indentation), so a search into the body lands. The reasoning text is itself surface area for search. What about the index? The heavy knowledge graph went almost entirely unread even in the condition where it existed. What supported reach was descriptive filenames, search into the body, and the standing rule that forces the check. If you're going to invest in an index, a light list of live decisions is as far as it needs to go. Where to put the check: a rule, a skill, or a template There are choices for where to put the check sentence. What I tested in the experiment was a standing rule with no path condition. This form belongs to the same always-loaded layer as writing it in CLAUDE.md (I didn't measure any difference in compliance by placement). Because it's always on the context, it works even for an ad-hoc request that doesn't go through the proper workflow. The silent restarts in the experiment happened on exactly that kind of request. On the other hand, the always-loaded layer degrades as it piles up. If you spell out the check procedure on the design-doc-writing skill's side, it loads into context only when needed, which is economical. The trade-off is that it only fires on a request that invoked the skill, and being read selectively, its certainty may drop. I didn't measure this form's compliance in this experiment. There's also a way to catch it from the artifact's side. Give the design-doc template a required "related existing decisions" section, and whether the check happened shows up in the artifact; if the section stays empty, a review can catch it. The only thing backed by measurement is the standing rule. If your always-loaded budget has room, the sturdy setup my data supports is to lay a floor with a small rule and also catch it from the artifact side with a required template section. Spelling it out in a skill is a strong alternative on the context-economy front, if it's a repository where design work reliably goes through a skill. Limits This experiment is a single personal-project repository, one model, three trials per condition — a small scale. Read it as confirming the direction of the reversal between conditions, not an effect size. I checked the validity of the judgments by re-classifying with a separate model blind to the condition (agreement 85% over 39 trials, κ = 0.72, all cells of the main conclusions matching). Still, uncontrolled factors remain. There's confounding from the agent itself holding knowledge of the tool under test, and the problem that a deletion leaks through Git history. Takeaways The value of accumulated context wasn't decided by whether it was written. It was decided by whether it got pulled out at the moment of conflict. In the previous piece, I wondered whether the prior research came up null because it measured scaffolding per PR. When I changed the unit of observation to "a decision, and a later request that conflicts with it," the effect became measurable. And once measured, the record itself is cheap (a few lines of verdict and status), while the reasoning text — thought to be expensive — earns its keep on efficiency and on search surface. The heavy index isn't needed, and the biggest lever was one sentence baking the check into the procedure. The karasu repository I used as the test bed is public, so you can read the actual ADRs I aimed at. The experiment environment, condition definitions, request prompts, and result tables for every round are collected in the notes companion. Follow-up: after this experiment, I put the check into my design-doc skill as a required step, the form I hadn't measured here. Four months later I looked at how it played out in daily use: Record What You Rejected, and Make Your Agent Check It: Lessons from 495 ADRs.

articles.title: How I built a free 3D landing page with Next.js, Three.js and GSAP
articles.description: I wanted a landing page where the product is the hero: not a photo of a can, but a real 3D can you can grab and turn. The result is Juicy, a one-page site for a made-up juice brand. Four cans sit on a wheel. Scroll, press an arrow key or click a button, and the wheel turns a quarter, the next flavour comes to the front, and the whole page takes on its colours. It is free and MIT licensed: Template page: https://www.aniq-ui.com/en/templates/3d-landing-page-template This post walks through the decisions that made it work, with the real code from the repo. The stack All versions are pinned exactly in package.json: Next.js 15.5 (App Router) and React 19 three 0.176 with React Three Fiber 9 and drei 10 GSAP 3.15 Tailwind CSS 4 next-intl 4, for English and Arabic 1. The wheel is plain DOM, only the cans are WebGL My first instinct was one big Three.js scene with four cans on a rotating group. I went the other way: four small canvases, one per can, placed around an ordinary div, and the div is what rotates. That keeps the 3D work tiny (each canvas renders one model), keeps the layout in Tailwind where it is easy to change, and lets GSAP rotate the wheel like any other element. Each can gets a slot at 12, 3, 6 or 9 o'clock: export const positionConfigs: PositionConfig[] = [ { className: "absolute top-0 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2", transformOrigin: "center center", rotation: [0, Math.PI / 3, 0], }, className: "absolute top-1/2 right-0 -translate-y-1/2 rotate-90", ]; The wheel itself is a 300vh square, so only the can at 12 o'clock is in view and the other three wait off screen: <div ref={wheelRef} dir="ltr" className="relative w-full h-full flex items-center justify-center"> {juiceCans.map((can, index) => ( <div key={can.id} className={`${positionConfigs[index].className} w-1/2 h-1/2 transform-gpu`} style={{ transformOrigin: positionConfigs[index].transformOrigin, willChange: "transform" }} > <CanvasContainer modelPath={can.model} rotation={positionConfigs[index].rotation} isActivePosition={index === activeIndex} /> div> ))} Note the dir="ltr" on the wheel. More on that in the RTL section. 2. GSAP turns the wheel, one quarter at a time The rotation lives in one hook. It refuses to start a new turn while one is running, and it only updates the active can when the tween finishes: Relative values ("+=90") mean GSAP never has to know the absolute angle, so the wheel can turn forever in either direction. 3. Mouse wheel, arrow keys and buttons, without double turns A trackpad fires dozens of wheel events for one swipe. A throttle of 800 ms turns that into one quarter turn. The keyboard handler also steps aside when someone is typing in a field (the page has a small sign-in form): isActive comes from an IntersectionObserver hook, so the wheel only listens while it is on screen. 4. One small canvas per can Each canvas is set up for a single object: device pixel ratio capped at 1.5, ACES tone mapping, sRGB output, a transparent background so the page colour shows through, and a lower power preference on phones. drei's PresentationControls lets you drag the can and snaps it back when you let go: <Canvas shadows dpr={[1, 1.5]} gl={{ toneMapping: THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping, outputColorSpace: THREE.SRGBColorSpace, antialias: true, alpha: true, powerPreference: isMobile ? "default" : "high-performance", }} camera={{ position: [0, 0, 1], fov: isMobile ? 24 : 22, near: 0.01, far: 100 }} {/* No fallback inside the canvas: the wheel stays hidden until the active can has loaded, and LoadingIndicator shows progress outside it. A drei fallback here throws a removeChild error when Suspense swaps it out. */} <Suspense fallback={null}> <PresentationControls global={false} cursor={false} snap={true} speed={isMobile ? 1.5 : 1} polar={[0, Math.PI / 10]} azimuth={[-Math.PI, Math.PI]} <Can3D modelPath={modelPath} rotate={rotation} /* ... */ /> PresentationControls> <Environment files={ENVIRONMENT_MAP} resolution={isMobile ? 2 : 8} environmentIntensity={1.2} /> <ambientLight intensity={10} /> <directionalLight intensity={20} position={[5, 5, 5]} /> Suspense> Canvas> That comment is a real lesson: a loading fallback inside the canvas looked tidy, but it crashed when Suspense swapped it out. The loader now lives in the DOM, outside the canvas. 5. Loading the GLB models The cans are four .glb files in public/assets/3d/can/. All four start downloading as soon as the carousel mounts, so turning the wheel never waits for a model: export When a model arrives, the hook clones the scene (so each canvas owns its own copy) and pushes the material towards polished metal: Only the can at the front reports "loaded". The page waits for that one, hides the loader, then fades the wheel and the fruits in. Nobody sees a half-built scene. 6. Idle motion belongs in useFrame, not in GSAP The cans sway gently while you look at them. That runs every frame, so it lives in React Three Fiber's useFrame, driven by delta so the speed is the same at 60 Hz and 120 Hz. On phones the sway is damped to 30%: useFrame((_state, delta) => { timeRef.current += delta * animationSpeed; }); My rule of thumb: GSAP for things that happen because the user did something (a turn, a text swap), useFrame for things that never stop. 7. Ship the lighting with the site drei's is one line, but it downloads the HDRI from a third-party host at runtime. I put the same file (Poly Haven's Forest Slope at 1k, CC0) in public/ instead, so the page makes no outside request and still works if that host is slow: 8. GSAP for the DOM around the 3D Two DOM effects use GSAP. The product text fades in when the flavour changes. The hook keeps a handle on the running tween and kills it before starting another, so fast clicking never stacks animations: tweenRef.current?.kill(); setDisplayedId(juiceId); tweenRef.current = gsap.fromTo( contentRef.current, { opacity: 0, y: 20, force3D: true }, { opacity: 1, y: 0, duration: 0.7, ease: "power2.out", delay: 0.1, overwrite: true, clearProps: "transform" } ); The fruits fly from the centre to their places for the new flavour and back to the centre for the old one. Each fruit's tweens run inside a gsap.context, and ctx.revert() in the cleanup undoes them when the component re-renders or unmounts: useLayoutEffect(() => { return () => ctx.revert(); }, [animationState, fromCenter, adjustedLeft /* ... */]); The page colour needs no GSAP at all. A CSS transition on body does it: 9. An Arabic version without breaking the 3D The page ships in English (/en) and Arabic (/ar). next-intl handles the routing, and the locale layout sets lang and dir on on the server, so the Arabic page arrives right to left in the first byte of HTML: <html lang={locale} dir={getDirection(locale)} suppressHydrationWarning> <body className={`${cairo.variable} ${anton.variable} antialiased`}> <NextIntlClientProvider>{children}NextIntlClientProvider> body> html> Two things went wrong the first time, and both are worth knowing if you mix RTL with a spatial scene: The scene should not mirror. Text and menus flip in Arabic, but a wheel that turns clockwise should keep turning clockwise. That is why the wheel has dir="ltr": the 3D part keeps its own orientation while everything around it reads right to left. Absolute positioning can resolve from the other edge. The wheel's container is very wide. With a fixed width and both left and right set, a right-to-left page resolves the box from the right edge, which pushed the wheel off screen. Placing it by top and left only fixed it: {/* Placed by top and left only. With a fixed width and both left and edge, which pushes the wheel off screen. */} <div className="absolute top-0 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 w-[300vh] h-[300vh] flex items-center justify-center"> Fonts come from next/font/google: Anton for the big wordmark and Cairo for Arabic text, both free. Run it git clone https://github.com/aniq-ui-pro/nextjs-3d-landing-page.git cd nextjs-3d-landing-page corepack enable && yarn install && yarn dev Open http://localhost:3030. With Docker instead: docker build -t juicy . docker run -p 3030:3030 juicy There is no .env to create: every file the page loads, the models and the lighting included, ships in the repo. Make it yours What Where Text in both languages messages/en.json, messages/ar.json The cans (3D models) src/features/carousel/constants/juiceCans.ts, models in public/assets/3d/can/ Colours per flavour src/features/product-showcase/constants/themes.ts Lighting public/assets/hdri/, set in src/features/carousel/constants/environment.ts Fruit images src/features/floating-fruits/constants/fruitImages.ts To swap a flavour, rename its id in src/types/juice.ts, and yarn typecheck lists every file you still need to update. What I would tell myself before starting Keep WebGL for the one thing that needs it. Everything else is easier as DOM. Preload every model the user can reach in one click. Do not put loaders inside the canvas. Self-host anything the scene fetches at runtime. In an RTL layout, decide on purpose which parts mirror and which do not. The repo is MIT, so take it apart, reuse the wheel, or swap the cans for your own product. If you build something with it, I would like to see it. If you need more than a landing page, the same team makes full Next.js apps (website, dashboard and NestJS API) in English and Arabic: websites from $39, dashboards from $49 and full stack packages at $149, paid once. They are at aniq-ui.com.

articles.title: Kubernetes - Setup External DNS
articles.description: This post is part of our ongoing series of posts for Kubernetes. In this post we are focusing on setting up External DNS, a critical component for automating DNS record management. Although we are working on a local Kubernetes cluster, we have implemented prerequisites in Kubernetes - Routing external traffic to local Kubernetes cluster to enable access to our internal cluster via public ip. We are using Cloudflare as our DNS Provider and implementing this solution using declarative GitOps principles with Flux. 1. Setup Cloudflare API Key First, let's generate an API key from Cloudflare by navigating to Manage Account > Account API Tokens in the Cloudflare dashboard. We'll choose Edit DNS template and generate token for a specific zone 2. Setup Kubernetes Secret Now we'll configure a Kubernetes secret by creating cluster/default/cloudflare-token.yaml Note: If you're unfamiliar with YAML path conventions and definitions, please refer to our guide on GitOps with FluxCD: Kubernetes GitOps with FluxCD - Part 1 - Initial Setup. apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: cloudflare-token namespace: kube-system type: Opaque stringData: CF_API_TOKEN: *** CF_API_EMAIL: *** Let's encrypt this sensitive data with SOPS and commit the changes to our Git repository. Note: For detailed instructions on secret management, refer to Kubernetes GitOps with FluxCD - Part 2 - Secret Management using SOPS. 4. Setup External DNS Now we'll configure the External DNS deployment by creating cluster/default/external-dns.yaml --- kind: ServiceAccount name: external-dns apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["services","endpoints","pods"] verbs: ["get","watch","list"] - apiGroups: ["extensions","networking.k8s.io"] resources: ["ingresses"] resources: ["nodes"] verbs: ["list","watch"] kind: ClusterRoleBinding name: external-dns-viewer roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment spec: strategy: type: Recreate selector: matchLabels: app: external-dns template: labels: serviceAccountName: external-dns containers: args: - --source=ingress - --domain-filter=*** - --provider=cloudflare resources: requests: memory: "64Mi" cpu: "20m" limits: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "200m" env: - name: CF_API_TOKEN valueFrom: secretKeyRef: key: CF_API_TOKEN - name: CF_API_EMAIL key: CF_API_EMAIL Explanation of External DNS Configuration This YAML manifest consists of four Kubernetes resources that work together to enable automatic DNS record management: ServiceAccount: Creates a dedicated service account named external-dns in the kube-system namespace This provides an identity for the External DNS process to operate within the cluster ClusterRole: Defines the permissions required by External DNS to function properly Allows read-only access (get, watch, list) to: Services, endpoints, and pods: To monitor for changes to service endpoints Ingresses: To detect new or modified ingress resources Nodes: To gather information about the cluster nodes ClusterRoleBinding: Associates the previously defined external-dns ClusterRole with the external-dns ServiceAccount This binding effectively grants the External DNS service the permissions it needs Deployment: Creates the actual External DNS controller pod with specific configuration: Uses the Recreate strategy to ensure clean upgrades Deploys the official k8s.gcr.io/external-dns/external-dns:v0.14.2 image Configures important command-line arguments: --source=ingress: Instructs External DNS to watch for Ingress resources --domain-filter=***: Limits DNS operations to a specific domain (redacted in the example) --provider=cloudflare: Specifies Cloudflare as the DNS provider Sets resource constraints to optimize performance: Requests modest resources (64Mi memory, 20m CPU) Sets reasonable limits (256Mi memory, 200m CPU) Injects Cloudflare credentials from the previously created secret: CF_API_TOKEN: Authentication token for Cloudflare API access CF_API_EMAIL: Associated email for the Cloudflare account With this configuration, External DNS will continuously monitor the Kubernetes cluster for new or modified Ingress resources. When it detects changes, it automatically creates, updates, or deletes the corresponding DNS records in Cloudflare according to the annotations and specifications in those resources. This eliminates the need for manual DNS management and ensures that your services are always accessible via their correct domain names. Let's commit these changes to our Git repository and verify that External DNS is deployed successfully. As we can see from the notifications in Discord, External DNS has been configured successfully. Let's examine the pod status as well: kubectl -n kube-system get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE coredns-ccb96694c-s67q5 1/1 Running 4 (60m ago) 4d2h external-dns-7cbfcc8d94-zwck7 1/1 Running 0 2m3s helm-install-traefik-8q42l 0/1 Completed 1 4d2h helm-install-traefik-crd-nq5tj 0/1 Completed 0 4d2h local-path-provisioner-5cf85fd84d-pxdcv 1/1 Running 4 (60m ago) 4d2h metrics-server-5985cbc9d7-qn4dr 1/1 Running 4 (60m ago) 4d2h svclb-traefik-aadbbe88-gjtbx 2/2 Running 8 (60m ago) 4d2h svclb-traefik-aadbbe88-vzd2t 2/2 Running 6 (60m ago) 4h10m traefik-5d45fc8cc9-g97pg 1/1 Running 4 (60m ago) 4d2h As confirmed, External DNS is up and running. Let's verify the logs to ensure proper functionality: kubectl -n kube-system logs pod/external-dns-7cbfcc8d94-zwck7 time="2025-02-28T11:26:25Z" level=info msg="Instantiating new Kubernetes client" time="2025-02-28T11:26:25Z" level=info msg="Using inCluster-config based on serviceaccount-token" time="2025-02-28T11:26:25Z" level=info msg="Created Kubernetes client https://10.43.0.1:443" time="2025-02-28T11:26:27Z" level=info msg="All records are already up to date" time="2025-02-28T11:27:27Z" level=info msg="All records are already up to date" time="2025-02-28T11:28:28Z" level=info msg="All records are already up to date" The logs indicate that External DNS is functioning properly. 5. Verify Setup Now we'll validate our setup by configuring an ingress for a sample application we created in Kubernetes GitOps with FluxCD - Part 3 - Automated Image Updates. First, let's configure a service by creating apps/sample-app/service.yaml kind: Service name: sample-app-service namespace: default ports: - name: http protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 8080 app: sample-app Next, let's configure the ingress by creating apps/sample-app/ingress.yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress name: sample-app-ingress annotations: external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/target: "******" - host: sample-app.*** http: paths: - pathType: Prefix backend: service: port: number: 80 path: / Since we're working with a local cluster, we've implemented a solution to route external traffic to our cluster as detailed in Kubernetes - Routing external traffic to local Kubernetes cluster. The public IP of our external server is specified in the external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/target. Now, let's modify the kustomization file at apps/sample-app/kustomization.yaml apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization - deployment.yaml + - service.yaml + - ingress.yaml Let's commit these changes and verify that External DNS has created the necessary DNS records: time="2025-02-28T11:42:34Z" level=info msg="Changing record." action=CREATE record=**** ttl=1 type=A zone=**** time="2025-02-28T11:42:35Z" level=info msg="Changing record." action=CREATE record=**** ttl=1 type=TXT zone=**** The logs confirm that the DNS records have been successfully created. Finally, let's verify access to our application using curl: curl http://sample-app.** Greetings From K8S App : Version 2 We have successfully configured External DNS, automating the creation and management of DNS records for our Kubernetes services. What next ? Future posts will explore advanced Kubernetes and GitOps patterns with FluxCD, including: Setting up Cert Manager Push based reconciliation triggers with Webhook receivers for FluxCD Stay tuned for each of these topics. References Kubernetes Documentation - https://kubernetes.io/docs/ External DNS Documentation - https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/external-dns/latest/ FluxCD Documentation - https://fluxcd.io/docs/

articles.title: Publish an App Inventor App on Google Play: Closed Testing
articles.description: Short answer To publish an MIT App Inventor app on Google Play, back up your keystore, set VersionCode and VersionName on Screen1, build an Android App Bundle and upload it to a closed testing track. New personal accounts then need at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before applying for production. To publish an MIT App Inventor app on Google Play with a new personal developer account, build an Android App Bundle (.aab) in App Inventor, upload it to a closed testing track in Play Console, and keep at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before you apply for production. Before any of that, export a backup of your App Inventor keystore. App Inventor makes building the app easy, but the Play side is the same for everyone, and a few App Inventor details trip people up: the keystore, the version code and signing errors on upload. Here's the whole path in order. Step 1: back up your App Inventor keystore first MIT's publishing page explains that every build is signed with a private key associated with your App Inventor account, and the same key signs every new version. The App Inventor server creates and stores it for you, so most people never think about it. Export it anyway. In the designer, the Projects menu has an Export Keystore option. Save the file somewhere safe, outside your computer too. MIT is blunt about this: if the keystore is lost or deleted, neither you nor MIT can recover it. Without it, you may not be able to ship updates under the same signing key. While you're there, also export your project as an .aia file from My Projects. It's your source code backup. Step 2: set VersionCode and VersionName on Screen1 Every app on Google Play needs a version code and a version name. In App Inventor you set both in the Properties panel of Screen1. VersionCode is a whole number that starts at 1. VersionName is the label users see, such as 1.0. Raise VersionCode by one every time you upload a new build, including builds for your closed test. If you forget, Play Console rejects the upload because that version code has already been used. Step 3: build an AAB, not an APK Google Play requires new apps to be uploaded as Android App Bundles, so choose the Android App Bundle (.aab) option when you build in App Inventor, not the .apk option. The APK is still handy for installing on your own phone. Older guides, including MIT's own publishing page, only describe building an APK, which is why so many App Inventor users get confused at this step. Fixing App Inventor signing errors on upload The most common upload problems in App Inventor's community forum are key errors, such as "Your Android App Bundle was signed with the wrong key" or "Use a valid app signing key to continue". They usually mean the bundle was signed with a different keystore than the one Play Console expects. For a brand-new app that has never been published, community volunteers report a fix that often works: export and back up the current keystore, delete the keystore in App Inventor, reload the browser, build the AAB again so a new keystore is generated, and upload that. For an app that's already live, don't delete anything. You need the original keystore, so restore it with Import Keystore. These are community fixes, not official MIT instructions, so keep your backup before trying them. Step 4: set up the closed test and your 12 testers In Play Console, create your app, fill in the store listing and the required forms such as Data safety and content rating, then go to closed testing, create a track and upload your AAB. Add your testers by email list or Google Group, and share the opt-in link with them. Google's rule for personal accounts created after November 13, 2023 is at least 12 testers opted in to your closed test for the last 14 days continuously. The clock only counts days when 12 or more are opted in, so aim for 15 to 20 testers in case someone drops out. Opting in is the requirement, but Google also asks about tester engagement when you apply for production. Testers who actually open the app and send feedback give you better answers for that form. App Inventor forum users have quoted refusals saying testers were not engaged, followed by a request for another 14 days of testing. Step 5: apply for production When 14 days are done, apply for production access from the Dashboard. Google asks about your test, what feedback you got and how you fixed it. If you shipped fixes during the test, mention them, and remember the higher VersionCode on each build. If you don't have 12 people who will stay for 14 days, PeerPlay is a free way to swap tests with other Android developers, and testers open your app daily from the app so each test day is recorded. Paid VIP packages are there if you'd rather skip the swaps.

articles.title: A Grading Race Condition: How to Avoid Evaluating an Outdated Submission
articles.description: How immutable submission revisions and an expected-version check prevent a grading form from silently applying feedback to a student's newer answer. A learner uploads an assignment. An instructor opens the answer and starts reviewing it. While the instructor is writing feedback, the learner finds a mistake and uploads a corrected file. What should happen when the instructor clicks "Save grade"? If the application simply updates the current assignment row, the resulting grade may describe a version the learner can no longer see. Nobody needed to act maliciously. Two legitimate users worked with different snapshots of the same record. This is a familiar concurrency problem, but educational workflows make its impact unusually visible. The answer, the attached files, the feedback, and the published result must remain understandable to learners, instructors, and sometimes guardians or administrators. Model a submission as an event, not just a mutable field A naive model stores the latest answer and the latest grade on an assignment: assignment ID; answer text; uploaded file IDs; grade; instructor comment. When a new answer overwrites the old one, the instructor loses the evidence of what was originally reviewed. A better model keeps immutable or append-only submission revisions linked to a stable assignment ID. A submission revision can contain its sequence number, answer text, the set of selected file identifiers, and the time of submission. A new revision is created only when the learner actually submits a changed answer. Existing revisions remain available to authorized participants. This does not automatically solve concurrent grading. It gives the server something precise to compare. Carry the version the instructor saw When a grading screen loads, return the revision identifier alongside the content. The client should send that identifier with the grading request as an expected revision. Suppose the instructor opened revision 4. The learner then submitted revision 5. If the grading request still says expected revision 4, the server must reject it rather than silently assign the grade to revision 5. The server response should explain that the submission changed and invite the instructor to reload. Crucially, the client can preserve the unsaved feedback locally while refreshing the work under review. This is optimistic concurrency: most reviews proceed without a conflict, but the server detects a stale decision when one actually happens. An optional expected-revision field weakens the guarantee. If older clients can omit it, the API cannot assume every grading request protects against stale content. During migration, document which callers supply it and what the server does when it is absent. The comparison must be atomic A common implementation error is: Read the current revision. Check that it matches the expected value. Write the grade. If another request updates the revision between steps 2 and 3, the check was correct at the time it ran but no longer protects the write. The comparison and the resulting state change need one concurrency boundary. Depending on the database design, that may be a transaction with a row-level lock or a conditional update that succeeds only when the revision still matches. A row-level lock serializes competing changes to the same assignment while allowing unrelated assignments to proceed. It does not mean locking the entire class or all learners. Be careful about attachments. Comparing only answer text is insufficient when revision 5 replaced one photograph with another but kept the same comment. Treat the submitted file set as part of the revision. Grading and publishing are separate product decisions Some learning products publish a grade immediately after an instructor completes the check. Others allow grades to be saved as drafts and published later by an authorized user. Neither model is universally correct. The problem arises when a user interface suggests one model while the server implements the other. A button labeled "Grade and publish" is clear if the result becomes visible immediately. In a draft-based workflow, the system should show the unpublished state and make publication a distinct action. Corrections after publication deserve their own history. Store who changed the grade, when, the old and new values, and the reason. If a guardian acknowledged an earlier grade, do not silently treat that acknowledgement as consent to the corrected result. How to test the race Use two independent browser sessions and a harmless sample assignment: In the instructor session, open revision 4 and start writing feedback. In the learner session, submit revision 5 with a changed attachment. In the instructor session, attempt to grade using expected revision 4. Confirm that the server detects a conflict and does not publish a grade for the wrong revision. Reload revision 5, review it, and complete grading through the intended publication path. Repeat with a client that omits the expected revision value. If that request is allowed, record the remaining risk instead of assuming every client receives the stronger guarantee. You can also test a repeated identical submission to ensure idempotence and check that two simultaneous grading requests do not create conflicting published results. The actual invariant The invariant is not "the latest row has a grade." It is "each grade can be explained by the exact work the instructor reviewed." Revision identifiers, server-side concurrency control, preserved attachments, and visible publication states are means to enforce that invariant. Once the system can answer "which answer was this grade about?", disputes become easier to investigate and ordinary corrections stop looking like corrupted records.
